title: Hall-Ready Gate for Liquid-Cooled GPU Tranches
one_liner: A fixed-price, 10-business-day release/hold decision, made 60-90 days before GPU delivery, on whether a liquid-cooled data hall will be energized and flowing when the racks arrive.
customer: Credit-desk principals and VPs at mid-market private credit funds, BDCs and specialty lenders on their first to fifth delayed-draw GPU facility to a sub-investment-grade neocloud, with no in-house commissioning bench. Secondary: mid-size AI labs signing take-or-pay capacity in a non-hyperscale hall. Excluded on purpose: hyperscalers and mega-funds that have their own engineers.
problem: In a delayed-draw GPU facility, the lender funds a GPU purchase order on the sponsor's word that the hall will be ready. That is roughly $3M+ per NVL72-class rack and hundreds of racks per hall. If the hall slips, the GPUs idle. My estimate is about $0.75M per day per $1B stranded (8% interest plus 5-year straight-line depreciation). Nobody on the lender's side is retained to say 'hold' at that moment. IEs certify construction draws. The technical advisors seen in GPU deals check fleet files, telemetry and power documents (per Peony). The RFS date is a sponsor sales number. NVL72-class racks have no air-cooled fallback, so the loop must be proven flushed, filled and leak-tested before any tray draws power. That work is done last, by scarce people. The parent's weakness was a broad 'better IE' pitch, sold through trust-gated relationships, with no software moat and an unproven right of site access. All of these are addressed below.
solution: One product for one decision, the 'Gate Memo'. It is $30K fixed, delivered in 10 business days. It has 12 binary hold-point tests, all in the failure zone: (1) written utility authorization to energize; (2) MV gear energized, with serials matched to bills of lading; (3) Cx Level 4 closed, with Level 5 IST script pass/fail counts; (4) CDU flush and pressure-test logs signed by the mechanical contractor; (5) punch-list burn-down slope over the last three weekly snapshots; (6) OEM startup technicians booked for named dates; (7) fiber acceptance; and five others. It also includes one site day by an ex-Cx lead and a probability of RFS by the sponsor's date. The memo ends in one of three recommendations: release, release with staged delivery, or hold N weeks. It is expressly not a certification. It does no draw certification, no cost-to-complete and no liability-bearing sign-off, and it leaves those to the IE. That keeps liability small and stops us from being an IE substitute. Access is solved with a free 'Readiness Rider', a two-page information-covenant and hold-point rider that finance counsel can paste into GPU facility documents. It gives the lender the evidence pack and one site visit as a condition precedent to each GPU tranche. The rider is both the access mechanism and the lead generator. After the gate, a $6K/month watch runs until RFS.
why_now: GPU-backed delayed-draw loans became standardized and large in 2026 (for example CoreWeave's $8.5B A3-rated DDTL closed 2026-03-31). That is pulling in mid-market credit funds that copy the structure without an infrastructure bench. Liquid-cooled racks removed the air-cooled fallback. Liquid-cooling engineers top a Q2 2026 US bottleneck index (Spencer Ogden, scarcity 80/100), and one missing controls technician can hold a finished hall out of service. Lenders are capping neocloud exposure and neocloud deals are stalling on credit risk. Satellite vendors have commoditized the exterior view, so the interior last 90 days is the scarce truth.
revenue_model: $30K per Gate Memo and $6K/month per hall for the watch. A retainer of $75K per fund buys 3 gates. Delivery cost is a 1099 Cx lead for about 4 desk days plus 1 site day, roughly $8-10K, so gross margin is about 65-70%. Year-1 target is 25 gates ($750K) plus watch fees ($250-300K), with about 6 principals doing the work. Year 2 adds a licensed benchmark dataset.
non_obvious_insight: The buyer is not purchasing a forecast. The buyer is purchasing an option trigger. The gate is timed to a decision with a cheap 'hold' branch (staged delivery or a 2-4 week deferral) and an expensive 'release' branch (idle carry). A false alarm costs weeks and a miss costs months of carry, so a forecast that is only about 65% accurate still has large positive value. This is why the lender does not need certainty and why the fee is trivially small next to the decision. Second, every gate produces structured data that IEs, who bill hourly and file Word reports, never accumulate: punch-list burn-down slope by hall, OEM startup lead times, and utility energization durations. After roughly 30 gates that becomes a reference-class dataset that sharpens each forecast, which is a process and data moat built from work you were being paid to do anyway.
first_30_days: Week 1: sign 4 retired or between-jobs Cx leads on 1099 contracts, prioritizing anyone who has commissioned liquid-cooled GB-class halls. Draft the 12-test Gate Memo template. Run it retroactively on 2 publicly delayed projects and publish the teardowns. Week 2: give 2 boutique finance law firms that do GPU facilities a co-branded Readiness Rider. List 40 mid-market credit funds with GPU or data center facilities, sourced from DDTL closing press releases and BDC filings. Weeks 3-4: hold 25 conversations with principals and VPs. Offer a design-partner Gate Memo at $15K on a live deal in exchange for an anonymized case study and permission to keep anonymized metrics. Target 2 signed by day 30. Riskiest assumption to test first: a credit desk will pay $30K for a hold/release memo that is not a certification. Test it with a pre-sale at day 14.
lineage: mutation of I0365 ('Ground-Truth Diligence for GPU-Backed Lenders'), type: sharpened
competition_context: Competitor check: GAP. Closest players: SynMax Vulcan (with Industrial Info Resources data partnership), Currence (formerly Sightline Climate), Epoch AI Frontier Data Centers Hub, SemiAnalysis (consulting, AI Datacenter Model, ClusterMAX). White space: The unserved wedge is narrow but real. (1) No product found in this session combines a binary, evidence-backed 'Readiness Ladder' for the last 90 days before RFS (utility energization letter, MV gear energization, Cx Level 4/5 and IST pass/fail counts, CDU flush and pressure tests, fiber acceptance, punch-list burn-down, OEM startup-tech availability) with a probabilistic RFS-by-date output and draw or covenant triggers. (2) Satellite and database vendors (SynMax, IIR, Currence, Epoch) cover the exterior and the announced schedule, and their materials do not claim commissioning or energization evidence. (3) GPU-deal technical advisors, as described by Peony, focus on fleet, telemetry and power documents rather than data hall commissioning. (4) Traditional IEs are slow, tied to a single lender or borrower, and priced for large project-finance deals. A fixed-fee, two-week, desk-plus-site 'second opinion' for a private credit desk, insurer or offtaker appears unserved. (5) The offtaker and backstop side (AI labs signing take-or-pay capacity, Google or Nvidia-style backstop providers) is structurally underserved because IEs work for lenders. Risks: incumbent IEs and Cx firms can add this as a service line, SemiAnalysis could bolt it on, and the business is people-bound (bench of ex-Cx leads) with limited software moat. Access to sites, contractors and Cx records depends on borrower cooperation, which means lender-imposed information covenants or offtaker leverage. | How this version avoids them: Traditional IEs: my search confirmed Sargent & Lundy markets data center owner's engineering, commissioning and performance-test oversight, and IE due diligence for lenders and investors, so this is a real incumbent. We do not compete for the IE mandate. We sell a 10-day fixed-price hold decision on one window, take no certification liability, and can sit beside the IE. Their hourly, multi-month, borrower-paid economics plausibly conflict with a small buyer-side product (hypothesis, unverified). SynMax/IIR/Epoch/Currence: their exterior and desk data are ingested as inputs and stop before energization and commissioning. SemiAnalysis: covers neocloud credit, pricing and operations, not hall-level readiness, and we do not touch GPU pricing. Peony-described GPU technical advisors: scope is fleet file, telemetry and power documents, so we own the pre-energization window. Watch for scope creep by them. Uptime Tier Certification: an end-of-build certificate, not a schedule decision. The narrow wedge (liquid-cooled halls, non-hyperscale sponsors, mid-market lenders) is also where large IEs' pricing and minimum engagement sizes fit worst.

title: Ruling-Backed Tariff Engineering for Product Brands
one_liner: A productized design-and-ruling service that helps mid-market brands legitimately re-spec products across tariff-line boundaries and locks the result in with a CBP binding ruling.
customer: Mid-market consumer and industrial product brands with $10-100M in revenue and at least $1-2M in annual duty spend: footwear, bags, apparel accessories, home goods, hardware, e-bike and powersports parts, and other products with metal components.
problem: Adjacent tariff lines can differ by tens of percentage points, and the 2025-26 regime made the gaps bigger. Section 232 metals lists keep expanding and being recalibrated, and copper smelt-and-cast reporting started July 30, 2026. Yet brokers are asked for a classification only after the tooling is cut and the design is frozen. Product teams never learn that a small change in materials, construction, packaging or set composition can legally change the line. Importers also avoid asking CBP for rulings, assuming it is slow or risky.
solution: Sell two steps. First, a fixed-fee HTS boundary audit: map the top SKUs to the classification tests, spec thresholds and comparable public CBP rulings that determine the line, and list the small design or packaging changes that would legitimately move each one. Second, an engineering sprint with the supplier that documents the changed product and files a CBP binding ruling request under 19 CFR Part 177. The deliverable is a ruling letter, which is a lasting shield for reasonable-care defense. Add a ruling-watch subscription that alerts brands when CBP issues a ruling on competitor or adjacent products.
why_now: The IEEPA reversal shifted the burden to product-specific tariffs (Section 232 and 301) where design details matter. The July 2026 copper reporting and the rewritten 232 valuation rules make product composition a compliance and cost variable. Brands are in a rare window when rate spreads are large enough that redesign pays for itself in one production run.
revenue_model: $4,500 boundary audit for five SKUs; $18-35k per engineering sprint including ruling preparation and filing; optional success fee of about 10% of first-year duty savings, capped. Ruling-watch subscription of $500-$2,000 a month.
non_obvious_insight: Classification turns on physical facts of the article as imported, and those facts are set by designers, not brokers. The most valuable document in a tariff war is a dull letter from CBP's ruling office, and requests cost nothing to file. Tariff engineering is legal when the product really changes, and it requires evidence, which is where a broker's habit of documenting everything matters. Trade lawyers do this ad hoc for large clients, but nobody packages it for mid-market brands at design stage.
first_30_days: Pick two verticals with high design freedom and large rate spreads. Use public CBP rulings to build a boundary map for a prospect's own top SKU as a free sample. Cold-email 40 product, sourcing and COO leads at $10-100M brands with their own sample map. Sell three $4,500 boundary audits and use them to select the first ruling filings. Sign a trade lawyer as reviewing counsel on the ruling requests.
lineage: original (tournament survivor)
competition_context:
Competitor check: GAP. Closest players: Tarifflo, Flexport (Customs Suite, AI Customs Classification, trade advisory, tariff refund claims), Zonos (Classify), Trademo (Global Trade Management). White space: Verified by fetches, with caveats below. No fetched page showed anyone selling a packaged, fixed-fee, design-stage (pre-tooling) HTS boundary audit for mid-market product brands ($10-100M revenue). None showed a bundled CBP binding-ruling filing with counsel review, or a ruling-watch product built on comparable-ruling analysis.

Software players (Zonos, Trademo, Descartes, Flexport) classify existing products. Tarifflo recovers past overpayments. Big-4 and law firms sell hourly advisory to large clients. A mid-market design-team buyer at the pre-tooling stage looks unserved.

Caveats that cap confidence:
1. The 200-call web search budget ran out before any search ran. Nothing was searched for boutique tariff-engineering consultancies, startups, YC or Crunchbase entries, Product Hunt, or open-source tools.
2. Several vendor fetches failed or returned thin pages: Altana, Avalara, Sandler Travis, Crowell, KPMG, Thomson Reuters, Expeditors and CROSS features.
3. So 'nobody does this exactly' is unproven. A specialist boutique or a well-funded new entrant may exist.

Structural risks that shrink the white space:
- Per 19 CFR 177.2, CBP rulings are limited to prospective transactions and require a full factual statement, samples and photos.
- Per 19 CFR 177.9, a ruling binds CBP only for the addressee and only for identical articles. Third parties cannot rely on it, and CBP can modify or revoke it without notice to anyone else.
- A classification ruling does not protect against Section 232 list changes. The lists are recalibrated and CBP treats sets by their primary classifying article. Redesigning across a line can be undone if the new line is later added to the list.

title: Outsourced Large-Load Intake Desk for Co-op Pools
one_liner: A stage-gated, applicant-paid intake administrator and cross-utility duplicate registry for G&T co-op pools outside ERCOT, so 5-person planning staffs only ever see evidence-backed projects.
customer: Wedge: one mid-size G&T (or state co-op association planning group) outside ERCOT, in SPP, MISO or the Mountain West, that fields 8+ large-load inquiries a year and has 1-2 planners eating the load (Central Electric Power Cooperative's lead spends about 40% of his time on data centers). The G&T adopts the desk by board resolution, and the applicant pays through a filed fee schedule, following Great River Energy's bill-the-petitioner model. Second ring: the G&T's 20-40 distribution co-ops, then neighboring G&Ts.
problem: The judges' central worry was right. Collateral, study fees and site-control rules are making applicants self-prove, so a 12-point memo shop sells checks the applicant will soon hand over anyway. Equipment slots and financing letters are also confidential, and real developers often call the utility before they order equipment. Meanwhile the co-op still has no staff to run intake and no way to see that the same 300 MW is being shopped to five utilities. Regulators are absorbing LLC transparency at the state level (Texas audit, Pennsylvania's Aug 18 order for projects over 25 MW), which weakens any pure-LLC-lookup product.
solution: Run intake as an operated service, not a memo. (1) Evidence ladder tied to money release. Gate 0 (intake fee paid): public-record checks only, which is what any real developer already has: LLC principals across states, recorded deed or option, air-permit pre-application and generator count vs. claimed MW, water and stormwater filings, and claimed energization date vs. published transformer and switchgear lead times. Gate 1 (study deposit released): named references (OEM, EPC, tenant, lender officer) verified by phone, with a signed attestation and a misrepresentation clause that forfeits the deposit. Gate 2 (ESA signature): redacted OEM order acknowledgment and financing confirmation. Early gates test only what an early-stage real project has; unobservable items are pushed to the gate where money is at risk. (2) Consent clause: the application form has the applicant consent to share LLC, principals, parcel APN, POI substation, MW ask and status with a pooled registry, which solves the confidentiality problem. The registry matches on parcel, substation POI and principal, not company name, because shells rename themselves but land parcels and substations do not. It returns hits like 'this parcel and principal appear in 3 other territories.' (3) Outputs are structured records that drop into GridUnity or PowerClerk as the pre-queue front door.
why_now: Tariffs and collateral rules are landing (Texas SB 6 final rule due by 12/31/2026, AEP Ohio-style deposits), and Exelon's pipeline fell about 40% and AEP Ohio's more than half once fees and collateral arrived. Every co-op now has to decide what its intake rules are, and most have no staff to run them. About half of announced 2026 builds are delayed or canceled, so boards are burned. Cleanview-class permit data has made the public-record layer cheap to assemble and license. Nobody yet runs a duplicate registry outside ERCOT, where SB 6 mandates duplicate disclosure only inside the state.
revenue_model: $20-30K one-time G&T setup (intake policy, fee schedule, ESA rider, board presentation). Applicant-paid intake fees scaled by MW, $10K under 100 MW up to $40K over 500 MW, plus a $15-30K Gate 1 verification fee. The utility keeps a 15% admin share and the desk keeps 85%. A $36K/yr G&T floor retainer covers slow quarters. Registry seats at $12K/yr for utilities outside the pool later. Bottom-up: 3 G&Ts x about 25 paid intakes x about $20K is $1.5M in year 1 at about 80% gross margin, with the registry as the compounding asset.
non_obvious_insight: The fee and the gates are themselves the phantom filter. Shell LLCs will not pay $15K to be verified, and real developers spending $2B+ will not blink. So the desk's real product is converting scarce planner hours into a queue that carries only evidence-backed projects, and detection is a side effect. The staged ladder fixes the 'real developers come before they order equipment' flaw by demanding equipment proof only at the gate where the utility's money is at risk. And the registry keys on parcels and POI substations, physical objects a phantom cannot rename, which is why it holds up even as LLC-disclosure rules improve.
first_30_days: Days 1-10: get the last 10-15 inquiries from two co-op contacts via a state association or G&T planning group. Back-test them to show how the ones that died would have scored at Gate 0 and Gate 1. Stand up scrapers for air-permit databases in 4-6 states and deed and Secretary of State records in 2-3 territories, and license Cleanview-style permit data instead of rebuilding it. Days 10-20: write the 2-page intake policy, fee schedule and misrepresentation-clause template. Present the back-test and template to the G&T planning head and ask for a 90-day pilot that starts fees on the next new inquiry, free for existing ones. Days 20-30: interview 5 developers with real projects to test that they would pay $10-15K at intake. Close 1 G&T pilot and process the first paid intake. Kill test: if no G&T will let applicants be billed, or 0 of 5 real developers accept the fee, the applicant-pays thesis is dead.
lineage: mutation of I0079 ('Phantom Load Vetting Desk for Rural Utilities'), type: sharpened
competition_context:
Competitor check: GAP. Closest players: GridUnity, Clean Power Research (PowerClerk), Enverus, LandGate. White space: I found no direct competitor. No startup, consultancy or association was selling a utility-side, per-inquiry 'is this developer physically real' memo with a recommended collateral amount and milestone-gated study structure. The gap is real but narrow.

What is unserved: (1) External physical-trail verification for small utilities, meaning air-permit generator counts vs claimed MW, recorded deeds and options, LLC principal cross-checks, and OEM or EPC evidence. GridUnity and PowerClerk track applicant-supplied data but do not verify it. Enverus, LandGate and GridCARE serve the developer side. (2) A cross-utility duplicate-request registry. Texas SB 6 mandates duplicate-request disclosure only inside ERCOT. Outside ERCOT there is no pooled registry. Developers do file the same project with several utilities (Latitude Media, Utility Dive). (3) Packaging for 5-person co-op engineering staffs: I found no NRECA vetting checklist or tool, and no small-utility-specific vendor.

Serious weaknesses the founder must address:
- Regulation and tariffs are substituting for vetting. Collateral, study fees and site-control mandates make the applicant self-prove. Exelon cut its estimates about 40% after stricter collateral. AEP Ohio's pipeline fell by more than half after study fees of up to $100K (https://techstartups.com/2026/09/01/ai-data-centers-request-700-gw-of-u-s-power-but-much-of-the-demand-may-be-an-illusion/). Once a co-op requires a deposit, site control and a signed LOI, much of the 12-point test becomes documents the applicant hands over.
- Texas SB 6 / 16 TAC 25.194 applies only in ERCOT (https://www.dlapiper.com/en-us/insights/publications/2026/03/texas-proposes-new-interconnection-standards-for-large-electric-loads). The 'small utilities in neighboring states get the displaced phantoms' claim is plausible but I found no evidence for it.
- Several tests may not be observable by an outsider. OEM order acknowledgments and financing letters are confidential, and real developers often approach the utility before ordering equipment.
- Regulators are absorbing the LLC-transparency piece. Texas ordered an audit requiring true-ownership disclosure, and Pennsylvania issued an August 18 executive order for projects over 25 MW.
- Big engineering consultancies could add this as a service line. I could not verify whether they already do. My web-search budget ran out before I could check. | How this version avoids them: GridUnity and PowerClerk are workflow tools built on applicant-supplied data. The desk verifies and feeds them as a front door, so it is a complement to sell alongside, not a rival. Enverus, LandGate, GridCARE and ZEG sit on the developer side or in forecasting, and this desk works for the utility and is adverse to the applicant. Cleanview is a public tracker and cannot hold confidential cross-utility inquiry data, so it becomes a licensed input rather than a competitor. NRECA offers free checklists but cannot run a fee-collecting, data-holding, liability-bearing intake operation, so its state associations are the resale channel. Hourly consultancies (Burns & McDonnell and similar) could copy the checks but not the pooled registry economics. Memos were the entry product; the pooled registry across co-ops is the business, and it gets better with every co-op added.

title: Warranty Gap Desk for MEP Contractors
one_liner: Sell to the electrical and mechanical contractors who promise owners a warranty from substantial completion while their OEM warranties run from shipment or startup, and fund the service from the contractors' own warranty reserves.
customer: The warranty manager, contracts VP or CFO at mid-size to large electrical contractors, mechanical contractors and construction managers building data centers who furnish the MEP equipment themselves (colo, enterprise and neocloud jobs, not owner-furnished hyperscale). They give the owner a 12-24 month warranty and carry a warranty reserve on the balance sheet.
problem: The parent assumed the owner feels the pain. The party actually squeezed between two clocks is the contractor. The OEM warranty passes through on an OEM calendar (startup or 18 months from ship). The contractor's promise to the owner runs from substantial completion or Tier certification, and owner-side counsel are actively advising developers to push warranty commencement to certification (the law-firm guidance in the parent's evidence). Every month of delay widens the gap, and in that gap the contractor pays for defects out of pocket. Estimators price it as a flat percentage, project managers do not track it, and closeout binders bury the OEM terms. Contractor warranty reserves are real P&L items the CFO wants released, which gives a budget line the parent never had.
solution: 1) Bid-stage gap pricing. Read the subcontract warranty clause and the OEM quotes, compute gap-days by equipment line, and price it into the bid instead of a flat reserve. 2) Deferral riders on the contractor's own POs. A contractor buying hundreds of units per year has leverage the owner lacks, and the desk pools rider purchasing across contractor clients for discounts. 3) Pre-expiry proof test and claim filing on installed gear so the OEM, not the contractor, pays for defects (load-bank partner does the physical work). 4) Reserve-release package at contract end: a documented file showing what OEM claims were accepted and what exposure remains, so the CFO can release reserve early.
why_now: Owner counsel now push warranty starts to Tier certification while long-lead delivery and phase slippage stretch the shipment-to-certification interval. Data center MEP backlogs are large, so contractors have more warranty exposure on more sites than ever. Extraction of PO, contract and OEM terms into gap-days used to require a warranty analyst per job and is now nearly free.
revenue_model: Program fee per project, roughly 0.03-0.08% of MEP contract value (about $120-320K on a $400M scope), which is a small share of a typical reserve. Assumption to validate: reserves of around 0.5-2% of contract value. Plus 20% of OEM-accepted claims that would otherwise have been borne by the contractor. Plus a rider-pooling margin or referral fee from OEMs and rental partners. Renewals follow the contractor's project pipeline, so revenue is recurring across projects.
non_obvious_insight: The contractor is the only party in the chain holding an unhedged, quantifiable, budgeted warranty liability, and it is growing because of owner-side contract trends. Selling to the contractor also flips the leverage problem: one contractor buys from OEMs at volume, and a desk representing several contractors can win start-date deferrals that no single owner could. The buyer is a CFO with a reserve, not an owner's ops team with no budget.
first_30_days: Call 15 warranty managers and project executives at regional electrical and mechanical contractors with live data center work, sourced through NECA and MCAA chapters and surety brokers who track contractor exposures. Offer a free 'gap map' on two live projects using their subcontract warranty clause and OEM quotes. Target: three pilots at about $25K per project and one signed OEM rider negotiation. Confirm the key assumption early, which is what share of their data center equipment is contractor-furnished.
lineage: mutation of I0229 ('Warranty Clock Recovery Audits for Idle Halls'), type: new-customer-or-model
competition_context: Competitor check: GAP. Closest players: Ethyco (data center commissioning, warranty-phase support), Anyset AI (agentic closeout / warranty tracking), Nomic (AEC document AI, closeout), Trane delayed start-up warranty (OEM rider). White space: Nobody I found combines all of these for data center MEP: (1) a serial-number-level clock ledger built for idle or deferred-start halls, (2) a pre-expiry loaded stress test using the idle capacity, (3) OEM claim filing and start-date deferral negotiation, and (4) success-fee or fixed-fee pricing sold to the owner or its lender. The pieces exist separately. Anyset and Nomic do doc extraction. Ethyco-style Cx firms do a 10-month warranty review. Wind and solar have end-of-warranty inspection and claims firms. OEMs sell delayed-start riders. Load-bank vendors have the hardware. Data center power and cooling MEP has no dedicated end-of-warranty claims specialist that I could find. Three structural weaknesses limit the wedge. (a) The clocks mostly start at OEM startup, and startup plus IST with load banks already loads equipment in Cx, so the 'idle for 12+ months' exposure is narrower than the pitch implies. It mainly hits gear started early or shipped more than 18 months before use. (b) 'Recovered value' is really avoided repair cost. It is hard to measure and easy for OEMs to dispute, and OEMs can deny on storage or light-load grounds (wet stacking is explicitly excluded, https://cliffordpower.com/wet-stacking-why-its-important-to-load-bank-your-diesel-generator/). A pure 25-30% contingency model will be hard to collect. (c) Documents are the commodity step, so the moat has to be inspection plus OEM leverage, not the LLM pipeline. | How this version avoids them: Ethyco and Cx firms sell warranty-phase support to owners after occupancy; the buyer here is the contractor, and the pitch is reserve release, not deficiency documentation. Anyset and Nomic sell closeout compliance to GCs and owners (is the warranty in the binder, does it match spec), while this computes the gap between the OEM clock and the contractor's obligation, buys deferrals and files OEM claims. Equipment Warranty Log and DCIM tools track expiry dates with no gap logic. Wind end-of-warranty vendors and Sinovoltaics sell to owners of other asset classes. Trane's delayed-start rider is an input purchased at pooled volume. WCS serves equipment dealers, not construction contractors, and is a possible referral partner. Aggreko and Sunbelt Solomon are load-test suppliers. Because payment comes from the contractor's reserve, the collection problem of a 25-30% contingency on 'avoided cost' owed by an owner does not arise.

title: Lender-Required Curtailment Reports for Data Centers
one_liner: An independent, productized report, like a Phase I environmental report but for power, that tells data center lenders how many hours a campus can legally run its generators when the grid curtails it.
customer: Debt originators, underwriters and portfolio managers who finance data centers where the lender carries power risk directly: neocloud GPU-backed delayed-draw loans, spec and powered-land developers without an investment-grade tenant, and ABS/CMBS arrangers and rating analysts. The borrower pays at closing, as it already does for lender-required third-party reports. Independent engineers and lender counsel are the channel. Start with PJM and ERCOT campuses.
problem: Every underwriting model assumes that if PJM or ERCOT curtails the campus, the on-site generators cover it. Federal engine rules and state air permits cap those engines at roughly 100 hours a year, with at most 50 for non-emergency use, and none of it can be run for money or under a financial arrangement. Texas SB 6 even states that it does not authorize violating emissions limits. A campus curtailed for 200 hours can be legally uncovered after 100. Lenders have no independent way to check this. The operator's own consultant is conflicted, and independent engineers are generalists. The exposure is real but unquantified, and it will be priced once someone quantifies it.
solution: A standardized 'Curtailment Runway Report', delivered in about five business days. It has four parts. (1) The permit-derived legal runway: per-engine hour caps, engine tier, allowed uses, monitoring and reporting duties, and remaining headroom. (2) Operational runway: fuel on site, paralleling and telemetry status, and the test and maintenance hours already consumed. (3) A curtailment-exposure distribution for the campus's utility and market zone. (4) A cost-to-cure estimate (permit modification, SCR, hour cap changes). Every report cites the permit conditions it relies on and is reviewed by a retained air attorney. A portfolio subscription adds permit-change alerts and annual surveillance refreshes. Campuses that score badly become inbound leads for the sharpened dual-mode permit service.
why_now: PJM's July 2026 auction was 6.8 GW short and its board plan lets large loads bring their own capacity or accept earlier curtailment. The curtailment rules are now credit terms rather than a policy debate. Texas SB 6 requires 75 MW+ loads to disclose backup generation and lets ERCOT direct deployment, so disclosure data will exist for the first time. Data center financing volume is large and recurring, and power availability is now the top diligence item. LLM-assisted structuring of permit PDFs collapses the cost of producing a first-draft report, while attorney review keeps it defensible.
revenue_model: $20-45k per closing report, paid by the borrower through the lender's third-party report budget. Annual surveillance refresh at $8-12k per campus. Lender or rating-agency portfolio subscriptions at $150-400k a year for unlimited reports and change alerts. Illustrative sizing to validate: 150 financings a year x $30k, plus 400 refreshes x $8k, plus 10 subscriptions x $250k, is roughly $10M annual revenue. Gross margin is high once permits are structured, because the same permit dataset serves every report. A white-label channel to independent engineers is a second line.
non_obvious_insight: The parent's permit dataset is worth more as a warning than as an unlock. Everyone else asks how much diesel can become capacity. The same facts show that the fallback everyone already assumes is often illegal past the cap, which is a downside risk with a faster buyer and no retrofit capex. Lenders reliably pay for independent third-party reports that gate a closing (Phase I environmental reports are the analogy, and the database company behind them proved the data business). Independence is the product. The operator's consultant cannot sell the same report, and aggregators profit from enrollment and have no incentive to say 'no'. A bad score also creates the demand the unlock business could never verify.

(3) A permit-headroom dataset across Title V and minor-source files.

The binding constraint is legal, not competitive. Under 40 CFR 63.6640(f), as summarized from Cornell LII, emergency engines are limited to 100 hours a year for maintenance, testing and emergencies, with at most 50 of those for non-emergency use. The 50 hours cannot be used for peak shaving or non-emergency demand response, and cannot generate income or serve a financial arrangement with another entity. Only narrow exceptions exist, dispatched by local authorities for transmission and distribution limits. Selling emergency-designated diesel as PJM capacity therefore likely requires reclassifying engines as non-emergency, which triggers stricter engine standards (Tier 4 or SCR-type controls), plus state NOx limits and possible major-source permitting. That is why the founder's 'retrofit the subset' step is likely the real cost and risk. It is also why incumbents have stayed away. The wedge exists only where the permit and retrofit math actually closes.

No competitor found in the parent's research sells to lenders, insurers or rating analysts.

title: Pet Claims Clearinghouse Starting at the Front Desk
one_liner: Invert the parent: instead of insurers policing vet invoices after the fact, give vet clinics a carrier-agnostic estimate-to-payout tool at the counter, then grow it into the standard transaction layer for pet insurance and a same-day payment network.
customer: Practice managers and lead client-service staff at independent and small-group US general-practice clinics (2-8 vets), and emergency or specialty hospitals where tickets run above $1,500. There are about 28,000 US vet hospitals. Later payers are pet insurers (per clean claim) and financing partners (per referred loan).
problem: An owner stands at the counter with a $3,800 estimate and says 'I have insurance'. It is one of about 15 carriers, the front desk cannot tell what will be covered, and the owner declines, delays, goes on credit or, in the worst case, euthanizes. Survey data shows 85% of vet professionals see owners decline recommended care at $1,000 or less, and they estimate about 13% of euthanasia decisions are driven by cost. After treatment, staff spend up to 30 minutes per claim in each insurer's own portal. Trupanion's VetDirect Pay shows clinics adopt this when it removes paperwork and lets them quote net of insurance (about 11,500 clinics as of October 2025, and a Digitail integration in August 2026), but it works only for Trupanion pets. Trupanion holds roughly 12% share in the market estimates found, so most insured pets have no such tool.
solution: Wedge product (shippable in about 10 weeks). Estimate Check: the front desk uploads the estimate or PMS export and the owner's policy PDF or insurance card. The tool returns per-line 'likely covered, likely excluded, needs records', a projected reimbursement range, and a one-page owner sheet showing what they will likely pay today and after reimbursement, with a financing option for any gap. It also shows the parent's edit logic turned around as provider-side scrubber tips ('these five lines are usually treated as included in the surgical fee; quote as a package price'). Claim Pack: after treatment it assembles the canonical invoice, records and the insurer's form, sends it through that insurer's intake channel, and tracks status. Network path: every estimate and reimbursement outcome trains per-insurer payout predictions. A published open transaction set (estimate, eligibility, claim, remittance on VeNom-based codes) is offered to insurers, who adopt it to cut intake cost. Later, an instant advance to clinics on insurer remits, funded by a warehouse line, turns it into a balance-sheet payment network.
why_now: Direct-pay proved clinic demand, but it is fragmented by carrier: Digitail and Trupanion announced their integration only in August 2026, and each new PMS-insurer pair is a one-off build. Insured pets are growing about 9% a year on a 4.27% penetration base, so the share of clinic estimates touched by insurance keeps rising. LLMs can now read arbitrary policy PDFs and messy estimates, which is what previously made a multi-carrier tool uneconomic. Corporate consolidation and price inflation make estimate conversations harder every quarter.
revenue_model: Phase 1: $199 a month per clinic location, sold on saved staff hours and higher treatment-plan acceptance, with a first-month free trial. Phase 2: insurers pay $0.75-$1.50 per clean canonical claim (their manual intake cost, an assumption to test), and financing partners pay a referral fee on loans originated at the estimate moment. Phase 3: 1.5-2.5% on advanced remit dollars (assumed range). Illustrative year-5 scale: 3,000 clinics at $2.4k is about $7M, 5M claims at $1 is about $5M, and $1B of advanced remits at 2% is about $20M, so roughly $30M of revenue on about a quarter of an estimated $4B of US claims paid.
non_obvious_insight: In human health, most claim edits run on the provider side, in clearinghouse scrubbers, before submission. Edits create value when they change behavior before the service, not when they reduce a payment afterwards. In pet insurance the only party who can renegotiate an estimate is the vet at the counter, and the only party with a real incentive at that moment is the clinic, because declined treatment is lost revenue. Flipping the parent's edits to the provider side removes its central risk (balance bills without vet contracts) and makes the vet a voluntary distribution channel. Whoever owns the estimate screen owns the transaction standard, just as the claim form did in human health, and the standard is worth more than any single edit library.
first_30_days: Week 1-2: recruit an ex-practice-manager co-founder and sit with 10 clinics, shadowing 30 insured-estimate conversations. Collect 200 real estimates with matching policy documents and reimbursement outcomes from 5 friendly clinics. Week 2-3: build the line normalizer and coverage rules for the top 8 carriers from public policy forms. Week 3-4: run a manual-assist 'Estimate Check in 15 minutes' service for 10 clinics by text or email, free, and score predictions against actual reimbursements (target: within 10% of the actual payout on at least 70% of cases). Convert 5 clinics to $199 a month by day 30 and ask the two most engaged to introduce their PMS account manager, which starts the marketplace-app conversation.

title: Independent Auditor for AI-Scribed Billing
one_liner: A continuous, coder-signed check on whether ambient AI scribe notes actually support the E/M levels being billed, before the payers or the government find out.
customer: Compliance officers, CFOs and revenue-integrity leaders at health systems and physician groups (20-500 providers), MSOs and PE-backed groups that rolled out ambient AI scribes. Secondary buyer: acquirers doing diligence on scribe-enabled practices.
problem: After ambient scribe rollouts, E/M distributions shift toward 99204-5 and 99214-5. Studies of six health systems show high-acuity visit share up roughly 12-20 points for new visits. Payers respond with AI downcoding and record requests, and the False Claims Act exposure is real if notes carry exam elements or time statements that did not happen. The scribe vendor cannot credibly audit itself, and annual compliance audits of 5-10 charts per provider cannot see systemic drift.
solution: Step 1 is a claims-only drift diagnostic (no EHR integration): compare each provider's E/M and modifier distribution before and after go-live with specialty benchmarks and peers, and rank the provider outliers. Step 2 is a targeted sample review by certified coders of the flagged encounters, checking that MDM or total-time really support the level. Copied-forward text, unsupported time attestations and orders without documented reasoning are the failure patterns. Step 3 is a continuing dashboard plus quarterly audit memos designed to be shown to a payer, auditor or the OIG. It includes a payer downcoding forecast.
why_now: Ambient scribes went mainstream across health systems in 2025-26. Research is documenting the coding-intensity increase and describing a payer-provider 'coding arms race', and payers are turning to their own AI for downcoding. The OIG's compliance program guidance expects organizations to audit new technology used in billing. Nobody independent has a standard offering yet.
revenue_model: $8-15 per audited encounter, or $15-30 per provider per month for the drift monitor plus sampled audits. Enterprise annual contracts of $50-200k. Diligence engagements at $10-25k each.
non_obvious_insight: The risk is not template bloat that scribes create in the HPI and exam. Under the 2021 E/M rules those elements do not count toward the level. The risk is that the scribe's fluent narration makes medical decision making and time statements sound stronger than what the physician did, and audits succeed or fail on MDM and time. Only coders who have survived payer audits know this. That is why a coder-signed audit is worth more than a model score, and why a compliance officer needs a third party, not the scribe vendor's coding module.
first_30_days: Find 3 mid-size groups, ideally with 30-100 providers, that adopted a scribe in the last 12 months, through LinkedIn outreach to compliance and revenue-integrity leads. Offer a free claims-only drift diagnostic, since 12 months of CPT data from their billing system is enough. Show them the outlier providers. Convert to a paid sample-audit engagement ($10-25k) and a monthly monitor. Recruit two certified auditors (CPC, CPMA) as contractors.

competition_context: Competitor check: GAP. Closest players: VMG Health (Compliance Risk Analyzer + AI Governance and Targeted Coding Audits), MDaudit, Healthicity (Audit Manager, Compliance Manager, E/M Analyzer/Utilization Benchmarking tool), Ambience Healthcare (scribe vendor with coding). White space: Nobody I found sells a scribe-specific, independent, coder-signed audit product. The gaps are: (1) An explicit before/after go-live drift baseline per provider, benchmarked against specialty peers and other scribe adopters. VMG's Compliance Risk Analyzer and Healthicity's E/M benchmarking do peer outlier analysis but are not framed around scribe go-live cohorts. (2) A review protocol built around what fails audits under the 2021 E/M rules: MDM and time attestations, not HPI/exam bloat. None of the vendor pages I read describe this. (3) An audit memo designed to be handed to a payer, auditor or OIG, plus a payer-downcoding forecast. (4) Independence from the scribe vendor, since Ambience, Abridge and DeepScribe all self-attest coding quality. (5) Scribe-agnostic coverage across a mixed-vendor group. Several legal write-ups recommend exactly the 'post-implementation baseline audit comparing AI-generated coding patterns against prior practice' (https://www.subjecttoinquiry.com/2026/06/ai-assisted-billing-could-create-fca-pitfalls-how-healthcare-companies-can-get-ahead-of-risk/), and none of the articles I read named a vendor that sells it. Caveat: this is a wedge in framing and packaging, not a technology moat. The existing audit firms and platforms (VMG, MDaudit, Healthicity) can run this same claims analysis and coder review, and could rebrand it 'AI scribe audit' within a quarter or two. My search was also incomplete, and startups from 2026 may exist that I did not surface.

title: GLP-1 Palate Panel for Food R&D
one_liner: A managed panel of GLP-1 users and their households that food and restaurant companies rent to test products, portions and health claims.
customer: R&D and insights teams at mid-size CPG (protein, snacks, frozen), restaurant chain menu teams, foodservice for hospitals and senior living, and supplement brands that need claim substantiation ($25-150k per study).
problem: 73% of GLP-1 users report taste changes and 70% lose joy in eating, so 'just add protein' fails. About 70% change what the household eats, and non-users adopt 30-50% of the changes, so the affected base is ~50% larger than the user count. Food companies are reformulating and launching 'GLP-1 friendly' labels on general-population panels and conflicting forecasts.

Run sensory, portion and format tests plus home-use tests and 8-12 week muscle and satiety claim studies. Deliver 'aversion maps' (which textures and smells trigger nausea at which dose) and household spillover models.
why_now: Households with a GLP-1 user doubled from ~11% to 22% in under 3 years. Pills launched in 2026 broaden the base. CPG is mid-reformulation, and FTC claim scrutiny makes 'evidence-backed' labels valuable. Purchase-panel incumbents see what is bought, not why.
revenue_model: $25-150k per study, plus $40-100k/year data subscription for 'aversion map' updates.
non_obvious_insight: The 'GLP-1 consumer' is 5-6 sensory segments that shift with dose and week on therapy, not one persona. Forecasting from sales data cannot separate them, but a panel can. The picks-and-shovels of a reformulation wave are the testers, not the brands.

title: Lead Line Photos Taken During Meter Swaps
one_liner: Add a 90-second, three-photo service-entry protocol with on-device AI to the water-meter change-out crews a utility already sends into basements, and sell it to the utility as a $10-14 per line change order.
customer: Mid-size water utilities (30k-150k connections) in the Northeast and Great Lakes that have inside-set meters, an active or planned meter or AMI replacement program, and more than 30% 'unknown' service lines in their inventory. Two budget owners: the AMI/meter program manager (capital project change order) and the lead program manager (compliance budget). The meter-installation contractor is the channel and co-beneficiary. Wedge account: a utility whose meter contractor has not yet mobilized, so the protocol goes into the statement of work.
problem: Unknown lines stay unknown because access is the hard part. Mailer self-ID reaches 10-25% of owners, and absentee landlords and LLCs almost never answer. The parent idea's paid-photo network has three weak points. First, opportunistic supply (home sales, water-heater swaps) is thin per utility. Second, the state may treat photos from third parties as self-ID-grade evidence, because the rule appears to require identification by 'water system personnel' (verify by state). Third, inspectors may not accept the liability of calling a pipe lead. Meanwhile utilities are paying crews to enter the very same basements and stand within about 3 feet of the service entry for every inside meter swap. Those crews record a meter serial and nothing about the pipe.
solution: An app or SDK for the meter crew. Photo 1 shows the pipe where it enters the wall, upstream of the meter valve. Photo 2 is a scratch and magnet close-up, using a $0.50 test card in the installer's kit. Photo 3 shows the meter serial and pipe together, which ties the evidence to the account. On-device checks reject blurry or ambiguous shots while the tech is still standing there ('retake, pipe not visible'). A vision model classifies the pipe as copper, galvanized, lead, plastic or unresolved. Low-confidence cases go to human QA and, for unresolved or mixed-material lines, to a probe or pothole queue. The tech never labels a pipe, which removes the liability concern. Output is a reconciled inventory feed in the state portal format, pushed into the utility's Esri layer, plus a dashboard showing unknowns falling by ZIP. Techs get a small per-verified-set bonus so they don't skip the step.
why_now: Meter fleets from the 2000s-2010s AMR wave are hitting battery and end-of-life, and cellular sunsets have pushed utilities into funded AMI change-outs (verify local schedules). These are the few funded programs that put a utility contractor inside every home in a specific neighborhood. State inventory updates and the 10-year replacement clock (federal details are still being litigated and revisited, and several states have their own statutes) mean unknowns carry real cost and a deadline. On-device vision models now catch bad photos at capture time, so the crew does not have to be an expert. SRF and infrastructure-law money rewards utilities that shrink unknowns before applying for replacement funds.
revenue_model: Per-line fee of $10-14 billed as a change order to the meter deployment contract, or as a per-utility deployment license of $60-150k. Change orders in that size range often clear without a council vote. Rough unit economics per line: installer bonus $2-3, kit $0.50, AI and QA $2-3, hosting and support about $1, leaving about $5-6 gross margin (roughly 45%). A 40k-inside-meter deployment is about $480k of revenue. Add-ons: inventory reconciliation SaaS, and later a resell of the same feed to meter contractors as a bundled 'verification-ready' option in their bids.
non_obvious_insight: The scarce asset is not a photographer, it is legal access. Every water tariff already makes meter access a condition of service, and utilities enforce it with repeat visits and shutoff notices, so meter crews reach exactly the absentee-landlord and LLC homes that no self-ID portal can reach, at a marginal trip cost of zero. The crew is also water system personnel or contractor, so the evidence sits in the strongest evidentiary class the state rule seems to allow. And the pipe at an inside-set meter is usually the same pipe the lead rule cares about, a few feet from where the crew is already working. A separate paid-photo marketplace has to build access, supply and trust. This borrows all three from the utility's own procurement.
first_30_days: Days 1-10: list every utility in two states that has inside meters, an announced meter or AMI program, and a public inventory over 30% unknown. Call the AMI program manager and the lead program manager at 15 of them. Also call three meter-installation contractors and ask whether they'd add a photo step for a per-set bonus. Days 10-20: get one state drinking-water program to say in writing whether a visual verification by utility-contracted personnel can reclassify an unknown. Prototype the capture app with real-time retake prompts and a scratch and magnet card. Days 20-30: run a 300-home pilot inside one utility's existing swap route, priced at cost as a change order. Validate the classifier against 100 lines the utility already knows (historical records, prior replacements) and against 20-30 potholes. Publish the accuracy and per-line cost, and propose a full-route contract at $12.

The parent's inspector network is dropped as the primary channel, which removes the cold-start, the liability objection and the third-party evidence problem.

title: Delay-Risk Underwriting Desk for Data Center Insurers
one_liner: Sell Delay-in-Start-Up underwriters a 5-day hall-level readiness review and a portfolio 'collision calendar' so scarce DSU capacity can be written on more projects with fewer surprises, funded by the insured through a policy subjectivity, and later share in the premium.
customer: Delay-in-Start-Up underwriters and engineering leads at construction and specialty carriers and Lloyd's syndicates, plus the construction-broker teams that place data center DSU, and reinsurers. The insured (sponsor or lender-as-loss-payee) funds the work through a policy subjectivity. Later: backstop providers whose payout depends on delay thresholds, for example a backstop that only triggers if construction is under about 180 days late.
problem: DSU is the most contentious and expensive element of data center construction cover. Zurich commentary says adding it cuts available capacity, and underwriters call it disproportionate to premium. A flood of AI data center submissions is hampering underwriters' ability to process them, and DSU capacity is being reserved for projects judged best risk-managed. Delay exposure can exceed $1B on a single campus. Carriers now require phased handovers and detailed commissioning protocols, and they ask who is building, what equipment is specified and how commissioning sequences, but they can only check documents. DSU claims later need programme evidence, commissioning records and contemporaneous project records that are rarely captured cleanly. Worst, DSU losses are correlated through shared scarce pools (OEM startup crews, CDU and coolant-chemistry lots, utility energization windows) that per-risk underwriting cannot see.
solution: Four layers, sold in order. (1) Pre-bind 'DSU Readiness Review' in 5 business days per submission: desk review of the commissioning plan and sequence, capacity check of the contractor and OEM startup technicians, the utility energization path, a stage-appropriate Readiness Ladder score, and an underwriter-facing recommendation on deductible, waiting period and warranty wording. The underwriter commissions it and makes it a bind subjectivity, so the insured pays. (2) In-policy monthly Ladder monitoring, framed as compliance with the commissioning-protocol warranty, with early warnings to the underwriter. It also builds the contemporaneous evidence file for any delay notice, which cuts adjusting cost and disputes. (3) Portfolio 'Collision Calendar' for carriers and reinsurers: how many insured halls need the same OEM startup crew or utility window in the same month, so accumulation is priced rather than discovered. (4) Year 2: delegated authority. We become an MGA or coverholder on DSU excess layers, or offer a readiness-triggered parametric top-up where a verified Ladder milestone missed by a date is the trigger, earning a profit commission.
why_now: Insurers began rationing DSU exactly as data center project sizes jumped, with average project value rising from roughly $150M to roughly $3M+ per the coverage above. Aon expanded its Data Center Lifecycle Insurance Program to $2.5B in January 2026, covering construction all risks, DSU and operational damage/BI. Brokers publicly call DSU the pressure point. GPU-backed lenders and offtakers increasingly want delay cover as a condition of their deals, which pulls more submissions into an already constrained market. Document AI now turns commissioning scripts, test reports and punch lists into structured evidence for cents per page, so a small bench can serve many risks.
revenue_model: $12-25K per pre-bind review, paid by the insured through the subjectivity. $4-8K per month per policy for monitoring. $75-200K per year for carrier and reinsurer portfolio analytics. From year 2, a 10-20% profit commission on DSU premium written under delegated authority, which creates outcome-linked economics: we earn more when our screening keeps loss ratios low. Bottom-up: 40 reviewed risks and 25 monitored halls in year 1 is about $0.8-1.2M, before any delegated-authority income.
non_obvious_insight: Underwriters do not buy diligence, they buy capacity. A credible hall-level score lets a carrier say yes to more DSU premium at the same loss ratio, so the buyer has a revenue reason to pay rather than a cost to minimize. Second, the pre-bind, in-policy and claims evidence needs are the same ledger, so one dataset serves three insurer budgets (underwriting, risk engineering, claims). Third, and most non-obvious, DSU is a systemic-correlation business disguised as a per-project one. Ten independently insured halls that all need the same OEM's startup crew in the same month are one risk, not ten. Nobody has the hall-level calendar to see it, and reinsurers will pay to.
first_30_days: Recruit 3 Cx leads plus one former DSU underwriter or claims adjuster as a paid adviser. Build a loss-cause taxonomy of about 6 delay causes from public litigation, insurer and broker commentary on delayed data center projects. Map about 20 DSU underwriters and construction-broker teams. Offer 8 of them a free shadow review, delivered in 5 days on a live submission with details blinded. Aim for 2 shadow reviews completed and 1 paid pilot by day 45. Insurance cycles are slow, so accept that. Riskiest assumption to test first: carriers will make an outside readiness review a subjectivity instead of relying on in-house or outsourced risk-engineering surveys. Ask each underwriter directly how surveys are commissioned today and who pays.

title: Contingency Recovery of Missed Rotable Repair Warranties
one_liner: A success-fee auditor that finds repaired aircraft components that failed inside the shop's warranty window, and turns them into filed claims and cash.
customer: Small and mid-size operators with their own stores and a thin materials team. That means regional airlines, Part 135 cargo feeders and air-ambulance fleets, and Part 145 shops that buy their own exchange units. They pay 20-25% of whatever cash or credit is recovered, and nothing up front.
problem: A repaired starter-generator, bleed valve, hydraulic pump or fuel control that fails 4 months after the shop visit is often covered by warranty. Almost nobody claims it. The tech pulling the unit at 3 AM is trying to make a 6 AM departure and never sees the warranty terms. The repair invoice sits in accounts payable as a PDF. The removal record sits in the maintenance system, and hours and cycles sit in a third place. One materials coordinator owns thousands of removals a year, with 30-90 day claim windows. Three other leaks go unclaimed as well: 'no fault found' evaluation fees on units that were still under warranty, unreturned exchange cores that turn into penalty charges, and repair turnaround-time guarantees that shops never credit because nobody compares PO date to receipt date.
solution: Ingest three exports: removals and installs, PO and repair invoices (PDFs read with an LLM extractor), and the negotiated warranty terms. Match by part number and serial number, including interchangeable P/Ns. Flag every in-warranty failure, late repair turn, disputable NFF fee and open core. Then draft the claim on each vendor's own template, track it to a paid credit, and re-run monthly. Add a 3 AM 'is this unit under warranty?' lookup for maintenance control, so the claim gets started at the moment of removal.
why_now: Airline cost pressure on regionals is high, and mechanic wages rose sharply in 2024-2026, so labor cost per removal is up. Materials teams are being cut while fleets stay old. LLM invoice and PDF extraction only became reliable and cheap enough in the last 18 months, and that is the missing link, because the money sits in unstructured AP documents that MRO software never reads.
revenue_model: Contingency fee of 20-25% of recovered cash and credits, with a 12-month tail on the audit. Later add a $2-5k per month SaaS tier for continuous monitoring, and sell benchmark data on shop warranty behavior to airline procurement teams.
non_obvious_insight: The leak is not in the maintenance system, it is in accounts payable. The tech who removes the part, the coordinator who could file the claim and the department that paid the invoice never share a screen. MRO software vendors will not fix it because warranty terms live in negotiated PDFs, not fields. Repair shops know most eligible claims are never filed, and they price that into their rates. A contingency auditor is the same playbook as freight-audit and telecom-audit firms, aimed at a niche nobody has covered.
first_30_days: Pitch 10 directors of maintenance and materials managers at small regionals, cargo feeders and helicopter EMS operators. Offer a free 12-month leakage audit, and ask them for the three exports. Build the matcher in Python plus an LLM invoice parser, and use a retired warranty or materials coordinator as a paid advisor for vendor quirks. Deliver a ranked claim list to the first 2-3 customers, file the claims yourself, and sign the success-fee agreement on the first credit memo. Publish the aggregate audit finding, such as the percentage of eligible failures that were never claimed, as the lead magnet.
lineage: original (tournament survivor)
competition_context: Competitor check: GAP. Closest players: Ramco Aviation (MRO/ERP software, warranty management module). White space: Caveat: this verdict rests on thin evidence. The WebSearch budget was exhausted (200 of 200) after the first two lookups. Every further search was refused, and I did not work around that limit. I could only fetch vendor homepages directly. I found no dedicated contingency-fee warranty auditor for rotable repair claims. I also could not rule one out, because I could not run Crunchbase, YC, Product Hunt or 'startup + key terms' searches. Vendor pages I checked (Trax eMRO, Veryon/Rusada, Pentagon 2000, CAMP) showed no warranty-claims features on their homepages, but homepage silence is weak evidence. I could not check IFS Maintenix (HTTP 429). Gaps that look unserved: (1) an outsourced, success-fee service that reads unstructured repair-invoice PDFs and joins them to removal records. This is the cross-system join the idea describes. (2) Small and mid-size operators such as regionals, Part 135 fleets and air-ambulance operators, which sit below the large ERP buyers Ramco targets. (3) The adjacent leaks, meaning no-fault-found fees within warranty, unreturned core penalties and turnaround-time guarantee credits. None of the vendor pages I read mention these. Unverified risks from my own domain knowledge, not from research: power-by-the-hour and maintenance-service-plan contracts remove warranty exposure for many small fleets. Shop warranty terms are often short and carry exclusions. Getting AP and maintenance-system exports from a small operator is hard. The addressable market may be small. Someone should check all of these before building.

title: Holdout Ledger: Landowner-Side Assembly Intelligence
one_liner: The landowner's half of the courthouse tape. It shows farm families and heirs in an assembly corridor who is buying around them, how close the buyer is to finishing, and how much leverage the last holdouts have, paid on closing.
customer: Owners of 100-2,000 acres in counties where recorded options and easements cluster, reached through ag and land-use attorneys, county farm bureaus, rural lenders and direct mail. Wedge: heirs, tenants-in-common and absentee owners who get anonymous offers under NDA. The payer is the landowner, on a contingent fee, plus subscribing law firms.
problem: Each landowner is approached alone by a landman working for an anonymous LLC. NDAs stop neighbors comparing notes. The developer sees the whole assembly and the owner sees one offer. Owners sign early and cheap, or hold out blindly, and cannot tell whether their parcel is a keystone or an afterthought. Landmen work for the buyer, local lawyers rarely have county-wide data, and county officials learn of the project from a leaked story.
solution:
1. 'Neighbor Check': enter a parcel or address and get a map of recorded instruments within about 5 miles, classified from the image. It shows the LLC family behind them, the share of the plausible footprint already recorded, whether the parcel sits on a critical path (contiguity, road access, a line crossing), expiring options, and a plain-English read of what the pattern usually means.
2. Owners in a cluster can opt into a negotiating pool, like the mineral-owner associations in oil and gas leasing. A licensed land broker or attorney partner represents them. We supply the analytics and take a success fee on closing.
3. We sell a group map subscription to ag and land-use law firms and farm-bureau chapters.
why_now: The 2025-26 large-load land rush has put anonymous NDA'd offers in front of thousands of rural owners, and local fights over data center land deals are widely reported. Owners can now see the buyer's footprint because public recorded memoranda can be read at scale with LLM vision. FinCEN's exemption for domestic companies means owners cannot ask who is behind the LLC and get a federal answer, so primary records are the only route. Reported prices such as roughly $100k an acre offered near Hill County, Texas, make the information gap worth real money to owners.
revenue_model: Free lookup as lead generation. $149-$399 for a full parcel report. A contingent success fee of 1.5%-3% of total consideration at closing, collected through a licensed broker affiliate. Example: a 300-acre owner closing a $4M option-plus-lease package yields $60k-$120k. $300-$800 a month per law firm or farm-bureau seat. Ten closed deals in year one is roughly $500k-$1M, at very low marginal cost after the data pull.
non_obvious_insight: The developer's own recorded memoranda reveal how complete the assembly is, and holdout value peaks in the last 20-30% of parcels. That is the moment owners are least informed. Every existing vendor's paying customer is the developer, so none can serve the counterparty without alienating buyers. That is counter-positioning in Helmer's sense. Landowners are numerous, each needs the service once, and assessor rolls are public, so mail reaches them cheaply. The demand is one-shot and high-stakes, which suits a contingent fee better than SaaS. The data burden is also small: a few dozen instruments per cluster, pulled per parcel, with none of the statewide bulk-ingestion risk.
first_30_days: Pick one county with a visible assembly. The parent's method of pulling 24 months of instruments gives the pattern. Mail 400 landowners within the cluster a letter with a QR code: 'Three LLCs using the same law firm recorded options on X acres within 4 miles of your land.' Offer a free Neighbor Check, then a $199 report. Sign a referral and co-marketing agreement with one licensed land broker and one ag attorney. Get 5 owners into a pooled negotiation and 20 paid reports. Before launch, have counsel confirm the broker-licensing and fee-sharing rules in the state (lawyers generally cannot split fees with non-lawyers), and use only public records. We are never a party to any NDA.

Everything I could read is adjacent. Parcel and ownership vendors (Regrid, ATTOM, Reonomy) sell deeds, mortgages and LLC piercing but not options or easements. Land-management vendors (Pandell, Enverus LandScape) manage a client's own documents. The main structural doubts I could not test are whether developers actually record option memoranda before announcement, and how many counties allow bulk commercial pulls of document images. | How this version avoids them: ATTOM, Regrid, Reonomy, PropertyRadar, Enverus, Paces, Cleanview, DC Byte, Heatmap Pro, GridCARE and Pandell all sell to developers, investors, utilities or the trade. None serves the seller, and none could do so without conflicting with its own customers. Generic land brokerages sell listings but do not read recorded non-deed instruments or unmask LLC families. Landman firms work for the buyer. Nothing in the research offers owners a cluster map or holdout-leverage view. The bulk-access risk is avoided because the work is targeted, parcel by parcel, within a county already showing activity. Weaknesses: a developer or its counsel may push back, some states restrict non-lawyer negotiation help, and reputation matters in small communities.

title: Bedside Coverage Recovery for Safety-Net Hospitals
one_liner: A pay-on-success desk that helps safety-net hospital financial counselors convert lapsed or presumptively covered patients into full Medicaid within the shrinking retroactive window, with informal-income evidence built over text message, paid a flat fee per approved case by the hospital's revenue cycle budget.
customer: Patient financial services and revenue-cycle leaders, plus hospital presumptive eligibility (HPE) and Medicaid enrollment managers, at safety-net, critical-access and county-owned hospitals in expansion states. Start in Nebraska and adjoining expansion states, where the state hospital association has already campaigned against retroactive-coverage cuts. The enrollee pays nothing. The hospital pays only when a case is approved.
problem: Two hospital-side facts changed. First, starting January 1, 2027, retroactive Medicaid coverage for expansion adults shrinks to one month before the application month (per Justice in Aging and other H.R. 1 explainers), so every day a lapsed patient waits to reapply can turn a billable encounter into charity care. Second, HPE screens for the work requirement by attestation and gives up to 60 days of temporary coverage, after which the patient needs a full determination, and hospitals are being urged to build conversion assistance. Projections cited by Applied Policy put FY2027 coverage losses at 2.3M, with about 43% procedural. The hospital sees the loss first: an inactive eligibility response at registration or the ED desk. But the counselor's usual application flow stalls on cash, gig and informal workers, who cannot produce payroll or wage records. The hospital eats the bill. (Assumption to verify: existing hospital Medicaid-eligibility outsourcers handle standard applications but not informal-income compliance evidence.)
solution: A Coverage Recovery Desk delivered as a light workflow, not an EHR integration. (1) Daily feed: a CSV or SFTP list of registrations with inactive or self-pay coverage and prior Medicaid, plus HPE patients at day 20 of 60. (2) Outreach in hours: hospital-branded SMS or WhatsApp in the patient's language. (3) Evidence build: the attestation and receipt engine from the sibling Cure Desk, with third-party attestations for cash workers. Patients who have a bank or payroll trail are routed to the state's own Emmy or SteadyIQ flow. Exemption triage and any state-optional excused months for inpatient stays are documented. (4) Retro-clock calculator: maps each open encounter to the one retroactive month and tells the counselor which filing date protects which claims. This is the hospital-specific feature, and the first thing they will use daily. (5) Counselor submits with a complete packet; we never decide eligibility. (6) Dashboard: dollars of self-pay converted to Medicaid-billable, by lapse reason. Digital-trail patients cost us almost nothing, so margin comes from doing the cash residual efficiently.
why_now: Jan 1, 2027 combines the work requirement, six-month renewals for expansion adults, and the retroactive-coverage cut, all landing on the hospital revenue cycle at once. Uncompensated care is already implicated in rural hospital closures. Hospitals are being told to strengthen HPE-to-full-Medicaid conversion assistance now. Cheap messaging, OCR and translation mean a counselor can handle several times more cases per day than with paper and phone tag.
revenue_model: Pay-on-success, no software fee to start: a flat $150-300 per approved reinstatement or HPE-to-full conversion, tiered by encounter dollars at stake. A flat fee per approval, not a percentage of Medicaid collections, because Medicaid billing-agent payment rules generally restrict percentage-of-collections arrangements (counsel to confirm). Optional $2-4k per month CFO analytics tier (self-pay at risk by lapse reason, retro-window leakage). Illustrative unit economics (assumptions to validate in the audit): a 150-bed hospital sees 120 lapse-related self-pay encounters a month, 25% are reinstated at $200, giving $6k a month or $72k a year per hospital, versus a Medicaid-paid stay worth thousands. 30 hospitals is about $2.2M ARR. Later: subcontract informal-income packets to incumbent eligibility outsourcers.
non_obvious_insight: The hospital registration desk is the earliest reliable detector of work-requirement and procedural terminations, because an eligibility check runs at every visit. Plans learn from monthly files, and states rely on notices that cash workers miss. It is also the moment of maximum patient motivation, with the bill in hand. Plans are limited to a supporting role under the IFR and MCO procurement is slow, but hospitals are neither plans nor determiners, and their counselors already file Medicaid applications every day. The cash-flow logic is lopsided: a $200 fee against a stay Medicaid may pay thousands for, and the one-month retro window makes speed a priced variable for the first time.
first_30_days: Send 15 Nebraska and regional revenue-cycle leaders a free 'lapse leakage audit': they share a de-identified 90-day list of self-pay encounters with prior Medicaid, and we estimate dollars at risk and how many are informal-income cases (procedural lapses today stand in for work-requirement lapses). Sign a BAA and a pay-on-success pilot with the first one or two. Run 20-25 live cases by hand: the counselor works from our SMS templates and packet PDF, and we track time to filing, approvals and the encounters saved by the retro-clock calculator. In parallel, ask the state Medicaid agency and a hospital association contact how reinstatement, reapplication and HPE conversion work for noncompliance terminations, and get counsel's sign-off on the fee structure.
lineage: mutation of I0573 ('Medicaid Hours Wallet for Gig Workers'), type: new-customer-or-model
competition_context: Competitor check: GAP. Closest players: CMS Emmy (Eligibility Made Easy) app and Emmy API, SteadyIQ (Income Passport / Verification Hub), Digital Public Works, Maximus, Optum, Acentra, Deloitte, Gainwell, Conduent, Curam/Merative (state-side community engagement modules). Nothing turned up in searches, CMS vendor pledges or CBPP/KFF/Georgetown landscape coverage. Vendors sit on either side of that gap. Findhelp sells eligibility-at-risk flags to plans, states and CBOs. mPulse and Propel do outreach and notices.
