The buyer is not an MCO, which removes the IFR supporting-role restriction and slow plan procurement. New risk not covered by the parent's research: existing hospital eligibility outsourcers. Mitigate by offering our packet builder as their informal-income subcontractor and by staying on the pay-on-success pricing they already understand.

title: Materials-Leakage Diligence for Trade-Shop Acquirers
one_liner: Sell search-fund, independent-sponsor and roll-up buyers of plumbing/HVAC shops a five-day report that reconciles the target's supplier spend to its customer invoices, sizes the fixable leak as EBITDA, and sets the baseline for a post-close capture program.
customer: Search-fund CEOs, independent sponsors and PE platform add-on teams buying residential plumbing, HVAC and electrical shops with $2-15M revenue, plus the SBA and ETA lenders and small quality-of-earnings shops that can white-label it. They are repeat or well-networked buyers who already spend on diligence and want a differentiated, quantified edge.
problem: Lower-middle-market trade deals are underwritten from a QuickBooks P&L and a seller-prepared add-back schedule. Gross margin looks acceptable or off, but the buyer cannot tell whether materials margin is real, leaking through unbilled truck-stock parts, or dragged by supplier price drift and stale pricebooks. Buyers discover the leak after closing, when the owner-operator's habits are theirs to fix. The parent idea has the same structural flaws sold to shop owners: owners feel a $10K fee is expensive and resist behavior change, and recoveries are hard to attribute. Generic accounting-firm quality-of-earnings work is done at general-ledger level, as far as I can tell, and rarely reconciles supplier spend to customer invoice lines, especially for shops this small.
solution: A fixed-scope, five-business-day 'Materials Truth Report' run in confirmatory diligence. The seller shares read-only QuickBooks and a field-service invoice export through the data room. The report gives (1) 24 months of Materials Capture Ratio (materials billed at cost divided by materials purchased) by job type, tech and supplier, compared with a pooled peer range; (2) supplier price position, meaning multiplier drift, surcharges and unclaimed credits versus the shop's own history; (3) truck-stock and inventory reasonableness; (4) a normalized gross-margin range for EBITDA underwriting; and (5) a 100-day capture plan with dollar values by lever (kit-based pricebook fixes, tech coaching, repricing file, supplier renegotiation). After closing, the buyer keeps the shop on a capture program measured against the diligence baseline, which was agreed pre-close and so cannot be disputed. Roll-ups get a portfolio dashboard comparing all acquired shops.
why_now: Tariff-driven cost swings since 2025 made materials margin the least trustworthy line in a trade shop's books, and buyers have been burned. HVAC and plumbing are consistently among the most-targeted sectors for search funds, independent sponsors and PE add-ons, so diligence differentiation is now a buyer priority. LLM parsing of supplier lines lets a two-person team deliver in a week what would otherwise be weeks of associate time. Field-service and accounting platforms expose exports, so a seller can share data in minutes.
revenue_model: Buyer pays $7,500 per target ($2,500 at engagement, $5,000 at close, or the full fee if delivered with the deal dead, negotiable). Post-close, either 20% of measured uplift over the diligence baseline for 12 months, or $500 per shop per month for roll-up portfolio monitoring. White-label to QoE boutiques and lenders at $3,000 wholesale per report. Value logic for the buyer: on a $6M shop, one point of revenue is $60K of EBITDA, worth roughly $200-350K of purchase price at 3.5-6x, so a $7.5K report is a rounding error next to the price adjustment or the 100-day plan value it produces.
non_obvious_insight: Changing the payer fixes three flaws at once. Authority: a new owner can change technician compensation, pricebook and process on day one, while an incumbent owner-operator rarely will. Attribution: the diligence baseline is a pre-agreed, third-party measurement, so uplift fees are not disputable. Willingness to pay: to a buyer the leak is enterprise value, not annual cash, so it justifies fees that would scare a shop owner. It also reverses the sales problem. Instead of selling to thousands of busy owners, you sell repeatedly to a few hundred networked buyers who talk to each other in search-fund and independent-sponsor communities, and each diligence adds a shop to the pooled benchmark without a per-shop sales effort. Roll-ups are the natural repeat customer and the natural distribution channel for the capture program.
first_30_days: Build a list of 40 search-fund and independent-sponsor buyers with live trade-shop deals (newsletters, ETA communities, LinkedIn, broker teasers). Offer the report free on one live deal in return for permission to cite anonymized findings. Aim for 3 live deals by day 30, with delivery within 5 business days of data access. In parallel, talk to two small QoE shops about white-labeling. Convert the first paid engagement on the next deal at $7,500. Position it as confirmatory diligence after an LOI, since sellers resist sharing invoice lines pre-LOI. Track whether the median target shows a capture gap worth more than $100K of EBITDA-equivalent, which tells you if buyers will keep paying. Web search was unavailable to the parent researcher, so first check for any existing tech-enabled trade diligence vendors.

title: Load Recovery for Municipal Utilities and Co-ops
one_liner: Sell the verified dead-plant record to the municipal electric utilities and rural co-ops that lose money every month the anchor plant sits dark, priced as a package plus a bonus tied to the load they get back.
customer: Municipal electric systems, rural electric co-ops and their joint-action agencies or statewide associations (for example American Municipal Power and the state municipal electric associations) in OH, PA, MI and IN, where an anchor industrial plant has closed and the utility's own economic-development or general manager decides. Wedge: 8 utilities in the Mahoning Valley, Akron/Canton and western PA with an idle plant of at least 2 MW in their territory.
problem: When a plant with several MW of load closes, a small public utility keeps paying its fixed wholesale power, transmission and substation costs but spreads them over fewer kWh, so rates rise for homes and shops and the remaining industrial customers get nervous (an assumption to validate with 10 utility managers). These utilities have no economic-development staff, are ignored by the investor-owned-utility databases and grid-analytics vendors, and cannot tell a data-center or battery developer what is actually inside the fence of their dead plant. Meanwhile the plant's energized service, which the utility itself installed and meters, is the one asset that could replace the lost load.
solution: A 'Load Recovery Package' per idle plant: (1) electrician-verified one-line diagram, gear nameplates, spare capacity and slab/crane condition; (2) the utility's own historical interval load and substation loading, which only the utility holds, turned into a stranded-load scorecard showing what re-energizing 2, 4 or 8 MW would do to fixed-cost recovery and rates; (3) a pre-cleared economic-development rate rider and a written will-serve position, drafted with the utility's engineer, which is the hardest input in the parent's product and is free when the utility is the customer; (4) outreach to a curated buyer list (manufacturers, battery and cold-storage operators, small data-center and inference developers) with the record as the data room. Later, a member-services version sold through a joint-action agency to all members.
why_now: Buyers with real money now want existing energized industrial shells, so a dead plant in a small utility's territory has more than one class of possible buyer for the first time in decades. Large-load tariffs and interconnection queues at the big investor-owned utilities push developers to look for capacity elsewhere, and roughly 128-week transformer lead times make existing service worth years. Ohio's 125+ local data-center moratoriums are a problem for pure data-center strategies, so a buyer-agnostic pitch to friendly municipal utilities is safer.
revenue_model: $9,500 per Load Recovery Package paid from the utility's economic-development budget; $18,000 per year retainer covering up to five sites, buyer outreach and a rolling record refresh; a capped performance bonus of about 10% of the first-year demand-charge margin from re-energized load (cap around $60k), structured as an economic-development services fee from the utility and not a commission on a property sale (have Ohio counsel confirm the real-estate licence question before signing). Channel: a joint-action agency or state association licenses the tool to members at $40k-$80k per year. Bottom-up: about 100-150 qualifying utilities in four states at an average $12k in year one is $1.2M-$1.8M, with 70-plus percent gross margin after the electrician cost on the package.
non_obvious_insight: The utility, not the broker or the manufacturer, is the party that already holds the two hardest inputs, years of interval meter data on the dead plant and the ability to say in writing what it would take to re-energize it, and it is also the only party that loses money every month the plant stays dark. Sell to them and the will-serve letter that costs the parent weeks of chasing becomes something the customer hands you. Small public utilities are also unserved by every funded competitor, which all chase hyperscalers and the big investor-owned utilities.
first_30_days: Week 1: build a list of every municipal electric system and co-op in northeast Ohio and western PA (from state association member lists) and match each to idle plants using Ohio EPA and county parcel data; shortlist 20 with a dark plant of at least 2 MW. Weeks 2-3: call 20 general managers and superintendents; pitch a free 'stranded-load scorecard' on their dead plant using their meter data. Get three to share interval data and access. Week 4: deliver one scorecard plus a paid quote of $9,500 for the full package, and pitch a 20-minute slot at a state municipal electric association meeting. Success test: one utility signs the $9,500 package or a letter of intent, and one association agrees to a member pilot.
lineage: mutation of I0820 ('Power Passport: Scoring Dead Factories on Amps, Permits'), type: new-customer-or-model
competition_context: Competitor check: GAP. Closest players: Brownfield.ai, Scout (ScoutCities), LandGate, Enverus Site & Screen. White space: Nobody I found productises a building-level, physically verified 'inside-the-fence' record for dead Midwest plants. That record would cover the electrician-verified main service size, voltage, gear age and nameplates, spare capacity, slab and crane-rail condition, the state of the existing air and wastewater permits, and a utility will-serve letter, all in a scored, comparable format sold before the deal. The funded players (LandGate, Enverus, GridCARE, Paces) work at the substation and grid level and are aimed at data centers. Utility and state databases (JobsOhio, AEP, FirstEnergy, ZoomProspector) verify sites and utility service, not building gear or permit status. Scout and Brownfield.ai are the closest competitors, but they look desktop- and network-led with no per-building inspection, and I found no evidence they carry electrician-verified data. The genuine gap is a trusted, standardised, seller-commissioned building electrical and permit record, not the parcel-scoring layer, which is already crowded and funded. The idea's weaker points: the Ohio permit-transferability wedge is thin (see evidence), and it is unproven that brokers will pay $1.5k-$3.5k. | How this version avoids them: GridCARE, LandGate, Enverus and Paces work at substation and grid level for data-center developers and large investor-owned utilities, and none inspect inside the fence. AEP, FirstEnergy, JobsOhio and ZoomProspector are free or embedded databases of sites and buildings that do not verify gear and are irrelevant to small public utilities without such programs. Scout and Brownfield.ai are network and listing platforms for buyers and owners with no utility-side product and no meter data. The customer here has no productised alternative, only the general manager's phone calls, and the utility's own data is a cornered resource the funded competitors cannot get at a small utility unless they are invited in.

title: SACCO-Financed Succession Desk, Paid on Milestones
one_liner: A white-label succession desk that payroll SACCOs offer their members: a check-off-repaid 'estate clearing loan' goes into a milestone escrow, and the company earns only as each case step is proven.
customer: The payer and channel is the mid-size payroll or sector SACCO (5k-100k members: teachers, health workers, county staff, police and prison staff) in central and western Kenya, sold to the CEO and credit committee. End users are two groups: salaried members (30-55) whose deceased parent's land is still in a dead name, and heirs of deceased members whose deposits and shares are stuck without a grant. The diaspora child is no longer the only payer.
problem: SACCOs hold two stuck pools. First, deposits and shares of deceased members that cannot be paid out cleanly until heirs produce a grant or agree among themselves (many SACCOs allow small nominee payouts; larger balances and family disputes stall; exact limits to verify): a governance headache, audit query and source of angry families. Second, living members who would borrow large development or mortgage loans against family land, but the land is in a dead person's name so the SACCO cannot take security. Members themselves cannot find a KES 100-250k lump sum for advocate, fees and travel, and distrust strangers who take money for land paperwork, yet they have salaries that can be deducted at source.
solution: The SACCO brands a 'Succession Desk'; the company runs it. Wedge (sellable in 30 days, no SACCO cash outlay): 'Deceased-Member Deposit Clearing'. The SACCO gives a letter of introduction and the list of stuck estates; the company does WhatsApp intake, heir map, consents and field work with a fixed-fee advocate panel; heirs consent in writing to a flat fee deducted from the released deposits. Stage 2, after three or more cases close: 'Estate Clearing Loan' for living members, sized KES 60-250k and repaid by payroll check-off. Proceeds sit in a SACCO-held milestone escrow released at proven steps: heir map and consent pack complete, petition filed and gazetted, confirmation of grant, transmission registered. Advocate fees (from a pre-agreed schedule) and the company's fee are paid from escrow to each party directly against milestones, so the member never hands cash to a stranger and the company never holds client money. At the end the SACCO has a pledgeable title (with heirs' consents to charge) and can pre-approve a development or mortgage loan.
why_now: Payroll SACCOs now run digital member ledgers, USSD and M-Pesa collections, and face competition from banks and digital lenders for their best salaried members, so they want secured, sticky products. Regulator attention on SACCO governance and deceased or dormant member balances (SASRA; verify current rules) makes stuck estates a board-level problem. LLM intake and heir mapping cut the cost of a case enough that a flat KES 12-18k fee works inside a loan. The succession backlog from 1960s-80s allottees is at its peak. Without cheap AI intake the desk would have needed paralegal armies, so this business model did not pencil out in 2019.
revenue_model: Contingent milestone fees of KES 12-18k per estate case, split over the four milestones (for example 40% at consents plus filing, 60% at grant and transmission), funded either from released deposits (deceased-member cases) or from estate clearing loan proceeds via escrow. The company takes no interest and no percentage of estate value. Flat per-loan bounty of KES 3-5k when a cleared title later secures a SACCO loan. After a successful pilot, a white-label desk fee of about KES 150-250k a year per SACCO. Illustration: 10 SACCOs at 100 cases a year each is roughly KES 15M in case fees plus about KES 2M in platform fees (about US$130k), with the SACCOs, not the company, carrying credit risk. The SACCO earns loan interest and clears a liability.
non_obvious_insight: Affordability and trust, not awareness, are the barriers, and the SACCO uniquely owns what neither an advocate nor a startup can: payroll check-off (repayment that costs almost nothing to collect), a welfare touchpoint at the exact moment of a death, and a balance-sheet motive (release stuck deposits, make land pledgeable). The estate clearing loan turns a scary lump sum into a monthly deduction, and the milestone escrow turns a scary stranger into a vendor who is only paid for proven progress. The SACCO's deceased-member float is an embarrassing liability nobody currently sells a fix for.
first_30_days: Days 1-10: list 40 SACCOs whose managers you can reach through personal, church, alumni and county networks (teachers', hospital, county-staff SACCOs first). Ask one question: how many deceased-member accounts are pending succession and how many shillings are stuck? Days 10-20: sign two advocates to a fixed-fee panel schedule and draft a one-page pilot contract: SACCO letter of introduction, member-consented flat fee deducted from released deposits, no SACCO cash outlay, so it fits within a CEO's delegated authority and does not need a board vote. Days 20-30: sign one SACCO for 15-20 stuck estates, start intake on the first 5 by WhatsApp, and publish an anonymised 'stuck member deposits' figure to open the next SACCOs. In parallel, draft the estate clearing loan term sheet with that SACCO's credit committee. Metric: days from intake to consents complete, and shillings released per case.
lineage: mutation of I0474 ('Dead Capital: Succession Kits for Diaspora Families'), type: new-customer-or-model
competition_context: Competitor check: GAP. Closest players: Luru (open-source 'Kenya's Digital Succession Copilot'), Wakili-Intel (AI drafting copilot for Kenyan advocates), Unclaimed Financial Assets Authority (UFAA), Ardhisasa (Ministry of Lands digital land registry). White space: Provisional, because the web search budget hit its 200-call cap before any search returned results. My evidence comes only from direct page fetches and GitHub repo searches. I found no funded startup, product or open-source project that combines (a) diaspora-paid flat-fee intake, (b) heir mapping across Kenyan name variants, (c) field-agent collection of chief's letters and thumbprint or video consent from 8-20 relatives, and (d) hand-off to partner advocates. The software pieces (family tree, readiness score, drafting copilots) exist only as zero-star hobby repos. Government platforms (Ardhisasa, court e-filing, UFAA) cover filing and claiming but not multi-heir coordination. UFAA's beneficiary claim rule makes succession a prerequisite for claiming a dead person's unclaimed assets, so a succession-first product that unlocks those assets has a logical hook. The unserved wedge is the coordination and evidence-gathering layer sold to the paying sibling abroad. It is still unproven whether ordinary advocates or land-buying-company agents already do this informally, because I could not search for them. | How this version avoids them: Fixed-fee advocates (the direct competitor) sit on the panel and are paid directly from escrow, so the desk is their referral source rather than their rival, and no fee is split with a non-lawyer. Luru and Wakili-Intel have no distribution, field agents or financing and are zero-star hobby projects. UFAA is unaffected because the desk clears the SACCO's own liabilities, not UFAA assets. Ardhisasa and e-filing are systems the panel files into. Competing on a different axis (who pays and how): individual advocates cannot offer financing or escrow; banks will not run rural field operations; SACCOs will not build LLM intake and consent ops in-house. Switching costs come from integration with the SACCO's loan system, panel and escrow, and it does not depend on the parent's unproven diaspora willingness to pay.

title: Store Takeover Truth Sheets for Lenders
one_liner: Buyers and lenders of Japanese convenience-store franchise takeovers pay per deal for an independent contract-aware valuation sheet that shows the store's profit after replacing the owner's own labor, under that store's actual royalty and disposal-share terms, plus the ordering upside a new operator could capture.
customer: The payer is the acquirer and its lender, not the incumbent owner. First targets are Kansai multi-store franchise corporations buying additional stores, first-time entrants and second-career buyers taking over a store, and the loan officers at regional banks, shinkin banks and Japan Finance Corporation branches financing them, reached through the founder's own lender and succession advisors. The seller supplies the documents because the sale depends on it.
problem: A store is priced off the HQ-issued statement of 'owner income', which blends profit with wages for unpaid owner and family labor (often 80 to 100 hours a week each) and hides how contract terms bite. At Osaka's 1,231 yen minimum wage, a couple working 140 combined hours a week is worth roughly 9M yen a year before any night premium or manager overhead, so a store showing 10M yen of owner income may earn about 1M yen for a buyer who must hire. A legacy 15/85 disposal contract also hands the buyer 85% of waste risk, while the seller's waste partly reflects HQ-pushed ordering the buyer can change. With Seven's 2027 new contract (50/50, lower charge) never converting existing stores, buyers must now choose between a legacy store and opening a new one on better terms. HQ approves transferees and earns royalties from whoever operates, so it is not a neutral source. Nobody independent computes either adjustment, and this removes the retaliation fear that makes existing owners hard customers.
solution: An 8-page Store Truth Sheet produced in about 5 business days from seller documents (12 months of HQ monthly statements, disposal totals, hourly sales, labor rosters, the franchise agreement). It shows (1) reported owner income restated as profit after paying market-wage replacement labor at current and scheduled minimum wages, (2) royalty tier and disposal-share mechanics for that specific contract, with sensitivity to wage and sales changes, (3) a range for ordering and markdown upside under the new owner's own payoff (the owner-side newsvendor model), (4) remaining term, transfer and renewal-risk flags, and (5) a legacy versus new-store comparison for buyers who could open a fresh store instead. Lenders get a white-label credit-memo version and a 12-month covenant-monitoring option. Later, buyers who close the deal are the natural first customers for the ordering product.
why_now: Three shocks landed together: the 1 Oct 2026 wage step in Osaka, Diamond's report of a Seven internal simulation showing franchisee profit falling to about a third under wage increases, and Seven's June 2026 announcement of a 50/50 contract from autumn 2027 for new stores only. That last one splits the market into legacy and new-contract stores and makes the price of a legacy store genuinely uncertain. Extracting numbers from photographed Japanese statements is now cheap, cutting a manual diligence review that would otherwise be a multi-week accountant job. The store-takeover market is assumed to be growing with owner aging, which needs to be verified before scaling.
revenue_model: 180,000 yen per store diligence sheet paid by the buyer (120,000 yen each when a buyer takes 3 or more stores). Banks that make the sheet a loan condition pay 40,000 yen per file or a per-branch annual license, and can pass it to the borrower. Covenant monitoring at 3,000 yen per store per month for lenders holding loans. Succession advisors who refer deals earn a 10% referral fee. At 10 deals a month this is about 1.8M yen a month, and every sheet adds a contract-parameterized store record to a proprietary benchmark.
non_obvious_insight: The same document set produces two adjustments that point in opposite directions and are both invisible to buyer and seller: owner income falls once labor is priced, and waste upside rises once a new owner uses his own payoff instead of HQ's. Both sides currently negotiate on the HQ statement, so the party with the correct pair of numbers can price a deal better than either side, and a lender will pay for that. Because the buyer pays and has no HQ contract yet, the product sidesteps the fear of OFC retaliation and the franchise-agreement third-party data question is limited to seller-provided records in a sale process. The by-product is a growing cross-store dataset of real royalty, waste and labor economics that nobody outside HQ holds.
first_30_days: Days 1-5: produce Truth Sheets for the founder's own three stores and note the gap between reported income and after-replacement-labor profit. Days 3-10: ask the founder's own lender for a warm introduction to 5 loan officers and reach 3 to 5 succession advisors and multi-store corporations. Publish a free 'profit after replacing yourself' calculator with 6 inputs as the lead magnet. Days 10-30: run 2 free sheets on live deals in exchange for a case study and lender feedback, then sell 3 paid sheets at 180,000 yen (540,000 yen) with a money-back guarantee if the buyer does not find it useful. Kill signal: no live takeover deals found among 15 conversations, in which case the segment volume assumption is false. Also verify seller and HQ data-sharing terms with a franchise lawyer.
lineage: mutation of I0272 ('Owner-Side Ordering: The Royalty Asymmetry Calculator'), type: new-customer-or-model
competition_context: Competitor check: GAP. Closest players: Seven-Eleven Japan AI ordering plus HQ-led markdown (Eco da Ne), Lawson AI.CO (ordering plus AI markdown recommendation), FamilyMart AI Recommend Ordering, Sinops (sinops-CLOUD AI markdown) with Sato. White space: No product found that is an independent owner-side payoff engine for Japanese convenience-store franchisees. Searches in Japanese and English returned no startup, SaaS or app that (a) uses the owner's actual royalty tier and disposal-share contract terms to compute order levels, (b) sets markdown timing from the owner's payoff, or (c) audits HQ AI recommendations against the owner's interest. HQ tools (Seven, Lawson, FamilyMart) cover order and markdown outputs but are HQ-controlled and aimed at waste or sales, not owner take-home. Supermarket AI-markdown vendors (Sinops/Sato, Wasteless) sell to retailers, not franchisees. The union and ex-OFC consultants give advice with no calculators or automation. The unserved wedge is: HQ says X, your own contract math says Y, the yen difference is Z, plus contract-aware multi-store economics. Caveats: (1) Seven-Eleven's new contract (announced June 2026, effective autumn 2027) raises HQ's disposal-loss share from 15% to 50% (with a cap), lowers charge to 53%/67%, applies only to newly opened stores with no conversion planned for existing stores (https://www.ryutsuu.biz/strategy/s061915.html, https://www.watch.impress.co.jp/docs/news/2118977.html). At 50/50 the owner critical ratio rises from about 22% to roughly 36%, so the asymmetry mostly fades on new-contract stores but persists on legacy stores for years. (2) Seven's HQ-led markdown push since 2024 partly commoditizes the markdown clock. (3) The 22% vs 70% math checks out for the 85/15 split, but contract terms differ by chain (Lawson subsidy formula is more complex, FamilyMart is about 15%), so each chain needs its own model. (4) Franchise-agreement limits on data use and third-party tools were not verified. | How this version avoids them: HQ AI ordering and markdown tools (Seven, Lawson, FamilyMart) are operational features with no role in a transaction, and HQ has a conflict as approver and royalty earner. Sinops, Wasteless, Afresh and Shelf Engine sell operations software to retailers and none values a franchise store. Too Good To Go is a surplus outlet. The union and ex-OFC consultants coach owners on markdowns with no calculators and do not sit on the buy side. Sell-side succession and M&A brokers were not covered in the competitor research and need a check, but by design they are paid on completion by the seller. The only independent buy-side underwriting of contract-adjusted owner economics appears unserved.

title: Independent Audit Samples for Modeled Lead Inventories
one_liner: Become the independent auditor of predictive lead-line inventories: sell engineering consultants and state reviewers a statistically designed sample of 60-150 photo-verified lines that proves a model's error rate, paid per ground-truth point plus an annual attestation fee.
customer: Regional engineering and environmental consulting firms (50-500 staff) that win lead-line inventory work as prime contractor, license or run a predictive model, and must defend the classification to a state reviewer. Wedge: firms holding three or more utility inventory contracts in a state whose drinking-water program requires field validation of modeled non-lead classifications, or in a state that rejects pure modeling (Texas is reported not to accept predictive modeling for official inventories, verify before selling). The state reviewer is the second beneficiary, and the utility is the eventual budget owner.
problem: Predictive modelers and consultants classify tens of thousands of unknown lines statistically, but a regulator or council will ask 'what is your error rate?' The consultant's current answer is a field crew, a subcontractor or potholing, priced at hundreds of dollars per point, with no independence from the party selling the model. Vendors that sell both prediction and verification are grading their own homework. In the parent idea the buyer was a utility that needed tens of thousands of lines cleared, which made low homeowner response and thin supply fatal. An audit needs far fewer points.
solution: An audit-sample service. We draw a stratified random sample from the utility's modeled bins (predicted non-lead, predicted lead, low-confidence), so the sample design is ours and can't be steered by the modeler. Homeowners get a utility-letterhead notice with a $25-30 incentive. A panel of 20-40 licensed plumbers and inspectors in the state visit and capture the three-photo protocol plus scratch and magnet test. Each point goes through AI classification, human QA, and tamper-evident geo-verification. Deliverables: (1) an evidence pack in the state inventory format; (2) an error-rate report with confidence intervals, including a non-response follow-up on a subset to measure bias; (3) a signed attestation the consultant can attach to the inventory submission. Where the state requires water-system oversight, the utility designates panel members as its agents in writing or witnesses by video. The sampling math is what makes it small: if 60 randomly sampled 'non-lead' lines are all non-lead, the true lead rate in that bin is below 5% with 95% confidence, and 150 clean lines bounds it below 2%.
why_now: First-round inventories leaned heavily on models, and reviewers, litigants and journalists are now questioning the unknown and 'non-lead' bins. The next inventory update cycle (around late 2027 under the federal rule, verify) is when models get challenged. Consultants are under fixed-fee pressure and want to avoid running field crews. Vision models plus tamper-evident capture make a small distributed audit panel cheaper than centrally staffed crews. Predictive modeling has reached the point where the constraint is credibility, not accuracy.
revenue_model: Wholesale price of about $140 per ground-truth point, against a cost of roughly $85-95 (panel payout $70-85, homeowner incentive, QA). An audit of one bin (60-150 points) is $9-21k, and a mid-size utility with three bins is a $30-40k engagement that fits under many small-purchase limits. Sold through the consultant as a pass-through with markup, or directly to the utility when the state reviewer requests it. Recurring revenue comes from an annual drift attestation ($10-15k per utility) as inventories are updated. A later product is a labeled, consented evidence dataset licensed back to modelers to retrain.
non_obvious_insight: A buyer that needs a sample, not a census, changes everything the judges worried about. Sixty to a few hundred points per utility means a 10-25% response rate is fine, thin opportunistic supply is fine, and per-point price can be $140 instead of $40. Every clean point vouches for thousands of predicted lines, so a sample point is worth far more to the buyer than a census point. The valuable thing to sell is independence: the model vendor cannot audit its own model, and the consulting firm that sells hourly field crews has no reason to keep the audit small.
first_30_days: Days 1-10: interview 10 regional consulting firms and 3 state drinking-water programs. Ask what evidence the state wants to accept a modeled non-lead bin, and whether a third-party photo sample with utility authorization counts. Pick one state and one consultant with at least three active inventory contracts. Days 10-25: recruit 20 licensed inspectors and plumbers through local chapters and pay a launch rate. Draw a random sample of 60 from one predicted non-lead bin the consultant has already produced. Mail notices with the incentive and contact until 60 are visited. Days 25-30: deliver the evidence pack and a one-page error-rate memo at cost or free, and submit it to the state reviewer through the consultant. Ask for a paid audit of the next utility's three bins.
lineage: mutation of I0463 ('Pay Home Inspectors to Find Lead Pipes'), type: new-customer-or-model
competition_context: Competitor check: GAP. Closest players: BlueConduit, VODA.ai (Lead Finder / Lead Zero / Lead Management Dashboard), Trinnex leadCAST (used by Durham, NC), Esri ArcGIS Lead Service Line Inventory solution. White space: Nobody I found runs the specific thing proposed: a paid supply-side network of trade professionals (inspectors, plumbers, water-heater installers) who photograph the service entry under a fixed protocol, with vision-AI classification, tamper-evident geo-verification, human QA, and export to state inventory formats, sold to utilities per verified line. Players fall into four groups. (1) Predictive modelers (BlueConduit, VODA.ai) reduce digs statistically but still need ground-truth field samples, and Texas does not accept predictive modeling for official inventories. (2) Customer self-ID portals (Trinnex leadCAST, Esri Survey123, Cognito Forms) collect photos and reach only the 10-25% of owners who respond, and absentee landlords and LLCs almost never do. (3) Hardware probes (Electro Scan, Echologics) need a utility crew at each line. (4) Door-to-door inspection programs (RCAP, engineering firms) are staffed centrally and slowly. The unserved wedge is professional-grade evidence for the non-responding, owner-absent lines at about $30-60 per line, collected by people already inside the building. Two sub-gaps stand out: states that reject modeling but accept documented visual verification, and small or mid-size utilities with no field crews. Caveats: (a) my WebSearch budget ran out after 4 searches, so Crunchbase, YC, Product Hunt and GitHub sweeps were not done and a stealth or very early startup in this niche could exist; (b) the search snippet says physical identification methods 'must be conducted or overseen by water system personnel' (state-dependent), so third-party photos may only count as self-ID-grade evidence unless the utility or state accepts contractor verification; (c) the idea's own note that regulatory details are from memory still applies; (d) per-utility supply is limited to home sales and water-heater swaps, so density per utility could be slow; (e) inspectors may resist liability for calling a pipe lead (my recollection, unverified); (f) Trinnex or Esri could add a 'contractor submission' role cheaply. | How this version avoids them: It sells to BlueConduit, VODA.ai and Stantec-type firms as an input rather than competing with them, and it is neutral where BlueConduit's own field partners or a consultant's own crews are not, which makes it a credibility layer. Trinnex leadCAST, Esri Survey123 and DIY self-ID forms collect voluntary owner submissions to fill the inventory, but none draws a random audit sample or produces a signed error-rate attestation. Electro Scan and Echologics hardware and RCAP door-to-door programs are verification methods that could be used as sample-collection tools, and a state may accept them, so they are potential partners rather than substitutes. A consultant or modeler that tries to build this in-house loses the independence that is the product. The parent's municipal sales cycle is replaced by consultants who already hold contract vehicles and small-purchase task orders.

title: Ground-Truth Diligence for GPU-Backed Lenders
one_liner: Independent-engineer-style diligence and monthly monitoring on the part of a data center build that satellites cannot see: the last 90 days before ready-for-service.
customer: Private credit funds, banks and ABS investors lending against GPUs and neocloud contracts; insurers underwriting delay risk; AI labs and enterprises signing take-or-pay capacity who need to know if the promised RFS date is credible.
problem: GPU-backed loans and offtake contracts are priced on a ready-for-service date. Satellite vendors (SynMax and Industrial Info Resources now cover 2,600+ projects weekly) can show steel, cooling towers and generator yards, but they cannot see the failure zone: utility permission to energize, MV switchgear energization, Level 4/5 commissioning and IST results, liquid-cooling flush and pressure tests, fiber-plant acceptance, OEM startup-tech availability. Percent complete on pay applications is front-loaded and misleading. Meanwhile GPUs costing millions per rack sit idle and depreciate while interest accrues, and lenders are capping neocloud exposure. Traditional IEs are power-plant-oriented, slow and expensive.
solution: A 'Readiness Ladder' of about 40 binary, evidence-backed milestones (utility energization letter, gear serials and bills of lading, Cx level sign-offs, IST pass/fail counts, CDU flush logs, open-punch burn-down rate, OEM startup-tech calendar). Score each project and re-score monthly. Output a probability of RFS by date and covenant or draw-release triggers. Staff it with a bench of ex-data-center PMs and Cx leads who do desk review plus quick site visits. Sell as a 2-week second-opinion product first, then monthly monitoring, integrating vendor satellite feeds as an input rather than competing with them.
why_now: Neocloud credit risk is now the topic. Lenders are capping exposure, deals are stalling on credit risk, and GPU-debt structures (including vendor backstops) are proliferating. Analyses show roughly 40% of AI data center sites with possible delays and about half of 2026 capacity slipping, while operators publicly deny it. Satellite monitoring has commoditized the exterior, which makes the interior truth the scarce and valuable part.
revenue_model: $25K fixed-fee 2-week second opinions; $40K-120K full pre-close diligence; $8K-20K/month per facility monitoring; optional success-based fee for delay-risk insurance placement. Adjacent product: retained RFS-credibility scoring for AI labs choosing between capacity offers.

title: Site-Control Check for Utility Large-Load Queues

customer: Large-load and interconnection managers, plus regulatory counsel, at G&T electric co-ops, municipal utilities and mid-size wires companies. Wedge: Texas co-ops, munis and mid-size TDUs (about 150 entities), then SPP and MISO states. The buyer is the utility. The applicant pays through the study-fee schedule.
problem: Utilities are buried in large-load requests, and many are speculative. The same parcel is shopped to several utilities. 'Site control' is often an applicant-supplied PDF or a non-binding LOI. The utility has to decide which requests get $100k+ studies and reserved capacity. A wrong guess strands capital or pushes cost onto ratepayers. Regulators and commissions now expect screening, but staff have no independent way to check control of land beyond what the applicant says.
solution:
The utility requires the applicant to list its parcels, and we do the rest.
1. Pull recorded instruments on those parcels and their neighbors from county portals, targeted per parcel with a landman fallback, so no bulk licence is needed.
2. Classify by reading the image rather than the clerk's label, and resolve the LLC family by notary, return-to firm and address.
3. Deliver a one-page Site-Control Report graded Recorded, Partial, Unrecorded or Conflicting. It shows acreage under recorded control against the acreage the claimed MW implies, option expiry dates, competing claimants, and duplicate-request flags across utilities through an opt-in hashed-parcel index.
4. Upsell a monthly territory sweep, which is the original Courthouse Tape, for assemblies that have not filed a request yet.
A human landman reviews every Partial or Conflicting result.

Texas SB 6 (2025) reportedly requires 75 MW+ applicants to show site control, disclose duplicate requests and pay study fees. Other utilities have added financial-commitment tariffs. ERCOT's large-load queue is reported at well over 200 GW, far beyond any buildable amount. LLM vision now reads messy recorded instruments accurately. FinCEN's exemption of domestic companies from beneficial-ownership reporting means LLC unmasking has to come from primary records. Verify the SB 6 details before quoting them to customers.

title: Plumber Parts Ledger: Margin Recovery Plus Failure Evidence
one_liner: Give plumbing shops a free contingency audit of unbilled parts, and pay them a bounty to bag failed pipes and fittings. The invoices become the installed-base denominator that makes the failure evidence valuable to insurers and manufacturers.
customer: Plumbing, HVAC and electrical shops ($1.5-15M revenue, 5-40 techs) as the supply side. Paying buyers are regional and mutual homeowners insurers' subrogation units and subro vendors, plumbing manufacturers and private-label buyers, and later distributors.
problem: Shops leak margin on parts bought but never billed. Plumbers also throw away the failed supply line or fitting that would have made a $9k water loss recoverable, because nobody pays them the four minutes it takes to bag it. Failure counts alone are weak, since manufacturers' lawyers can dismiss them without knowing how many units were sold, installed and stayed fine.
solution: Shops forward supply-house invoices and give a field-service export. An LLM parser ties invoice lines to jobs and returns a weekly leak list, paid at 25% of recovered revenue, with no fee if nothing is found. The same app hands out tamper-evident QR bags. A 90-second phone flow captures photo in place, date code, homeowner e-signature and claim number, and a weekly courier pickup delivers chain-of-custody parts. Each bag is auto-linked to the job's SKU, install date and installer from the invoice ledger. Outputs are subrogation evidence packs, per-SKU failure-rate reports (failures per 10,000 units sold), and at-risk-address lists for proactive replacement.
why_now: Water damage is one of the top two homeowner claim categories, and insurers are squeezed enough that routine $8-15k losses are never pursued. LLM invoice parsing now works on messy supply-house PDFs and photos, which made both products cheap enough for a two-person team.
revenue_model: 25% of recovered and newly captured revenue for 12 months, converting to $199-499 per month monitoring. $75-150 per bagged part from insurers or subro vendors (of which $40-60 goes to the shop and tech), plus a 3-8% success share on recoveries. $15-60k per year failure-data licenses to manufacturers and distributors. Later, per-address replacement programs sold to insurers as loss prevention.
non_obvious_insight: The denominator only exists in the shop's invoices, and it arrives as a byproduct of margin recovery. It converts anecdotes into rates manufacturers can't wave away. It also identifies who installed which SKU at which address and when, which decides warranty windows and statute of repose. The installed-base list is the real prize: when a lot goes bad, the insurer can pay $15 to replace a braided line at every address that received it, instead of paying $9k after it bursts.
first_30_days: Recruit 10 shops through a local PHCC chapter and owner peer groups with a free 90-day audit and a free evidence kit. Turn each audit around in 48 hours with a single 'found money' number. Pay a flat $50 per bag and collect the first 50 parts with photos. Link each part to its invoice line. Take 20 case files to two regional mutual insurers and a subro vendor and sell a 100-part paid pilot.

The bounty alone has a cold-start problem: shops have no reason to stay engaged and the data has no denominator. Together, the free audit is the near-zero-CAC hook into the same shops, the bounty gives them a second paycheck, and the joined install-and-failure ledger is a dataset neither ServiceTitan nor a forensic firm can assemble.

Competitor check: GAP. Closest players: Donan Engineering - Loss Logistics, Envista Forensics and Rimkus (forensic engineering / property loss consulting), LeakBot, ServiceTitan and CompanyCam (plumber field software). I did not check Crunchbase, YC, Product Hunt or trade press, so I could not rule out a small funded startup doing exactly this. Run 4-6 searches before committing money. Insurer-funded plumber networks exist (LeakBot). Plumber field software exists (ServiceTitan, CompanyCam). No page I read describes any of these paying or equipping the plumber to retain the failed part on routine sub-$15k water losses. The public failure data I found is weak (SaferProducts.gov). title: Tooling Title Diligence for Small-Brand Acquirers
one_liner: A fixed-fee, 5-day report that tells buyers of $2M-$50M product companies which molds the target legally owns, where they physically sit, and whether the factory is already selling the target's product.
customer: Buyers of physical-product brands and small manufacturers with China-made tooling: search-fund and ETA searchers, independent sponsors, lower-mid-market PE platforms and SBA 7(a) acquirers. The channel is business brokers (Quiet Light, Empire Flippers, FE International-type firms), M&A attorneys and SBA acquisition lenders. The payer is the buyer, at the LOI-to-close stage. Secondary payer is the seller, who pays for a pre-listing 'tooling-ready' file.
problem: In a small-brand acquisition the molds are the asset that everyone values at zero. The QoE accountant sees an expensed PO line, the lawyer sees a boilerplate 'all assets used in the business' rep, and the seller often cannot say whose name the tools are in or whether a bill of sale exists. If the factory holds the tools, the buyer has bought a business that the supplier can hold hostage for a 30% price hike, and the buyer also cannot move production, which matters more now that tariff rules keep changing. Nobody in the deal owns this question: brand-protection vendors sell to the brand, not to the buyer, and audit firms do not cover tooling.
solution: 'Tooling Title and Leakage Report', delivered in 5 business days. (1) Tool schedule: every tool, its location, its condition, and who holds title (bill of sale, PO language, tool-ownership clauses, supplier confirmation letters). (2) Leakage test, which is the parent's $2,500 overrun audit repurposed: buy 10 units from 1688, Alibaba, Temu and Amazon third-party sellers, and compare them with the golden sample and lot codes to say whether the supplier is already selling the product. (3) Portability score: what it would cost and how long it would take to move each tool or re-cut it, with quotes from a US or Mexican molder. (4) Deal remedies: draft closing conditions, a tool bill-of-sale assignment, custody and release agreements, and a holdback or escrow sizing suggestion for the buyer's lawyer to use. The on-site audit is optional and subcontracted, passed through at cost, and only for deals over $10M.
why_now: The searcher and ETA wave and retiring owners are pushing more small manufacturers and brands to market. The Amazon aggregator unwinding put many product brands up for resale with tooling and supplier problems. Tariff volatility (the Feb 2026 IEEPA ruling per the parent research) makes 'can this brand switch factories?' a live diligence question, where in 2019 it was rarely asked. Remote marketplace scanning has become cheap enough to fit inside a fixed fee.
revenue_model: $4,900 per report, paid by the buyer, usually as a closing cost. Seller pre-listing file $2,500 through brokers. Post-close '100-day tool sovereignty plan' $12k (title cure, fingerprint baseline, second-source quotes). Portfolio monitoring for PE sponsors $2,000/month per physical-product company. Model: 240 reports a year at month 12 is about $1.2M, plus a 25% attach rate on the plan (60 plans at $12k) is about $0.7M. Reachable market is assumed at roughly 1,500 physical-product deals a year, to be validated with brokers. Lenders or brokers might pay for reports on deals that later close.
non_obvious_insight: This is the same asset as the parent idea, but a far better moment to sell it. A breakup victim only hires you once they are already hurt and have already lost leverage. An acquirer is at peak willingness to pay, because they are about to wire $5M, and the report's cost is rounding error on the deal. The finding also turns straight into money: a missing bill of sale becomes a closing condition, a holdback or a price cut. A short-lived supplier concentration risk becomes a negotiating chip. Diligence is also the top of a repeat-customer funnel, since a sponsor with 6 platform companies buys monitoring on all of them.
first_30_days: Build a redacted sample report from public listings and a mock data room. Pitch 6 brokers and 3 searcher communities, offering 3 free reports on live deals, in exchange for testimonials and a written referral agreement, since a diligence step that reduces buyer fear helps brokers close deals. Then sell 5 paid reports at an introductory $3,500. Get one M&A attorney to endorse the closing-condition language. Line up two China audit contractors by referral for the on-site option. Kill signal: brokers refuse to introduce the report to buyers, or no buyer will pay $3.5k.

title: ITAR-Safe Identity for New-Space Startups
one_liner: An identity layer that proves a new hire is real, where they actually are and whether they may legally see spacecraft technical data, then feeds that attribute straight into SSO and PLM access controls.
customer: Series A-C launch, satellite and defense-space startups (50-500 staff) and their sub-tier machine shops and avionics suppliers, reached through space-focused investors, accelerators and SpaceWERX/SBIR cohorts. Buyers are the head of security or compliance and the CFO.
problem: Space startups are hiring at breakneck speed, with remote engineers and contractors, into a Golden Dome-driven market (cost estimate raised to $185B) and nine-figure funding rounds. Giving a foreign person access to technical data is an ITAR export violation, and North Korean IT-worker schemes have reached 70 to 100+ US companies. Standard IDV proves someone is real, not whether they are a US person, and HR and ATS tools do not carry export-control eligibility as an access attribute. Fake suppliers and counterfeit parts add a second exposure.
solution: (1) Verify person and US-person status using document and injection-resistant liveness (partner with an existing IDV vendor rather than building it). (2) Check presence over time (VPN and laptop-farm signals). (3) Write 'US person, permitted data categories' into Okta or Entra groups and PLM and repo permissions through SCIM. (4) Supplier onboarding with KYB, sanctions and counterfeit-part red flags. (5) An auditor-ready evidence pack for CMMC Level 2 assessments and export-compliance reviews.
why_now: The DoD's CMMC rollout reaches its second phase on 10 Nov 2026, when third-party Level 2 certification starts appearing in contracts, and small suppliers are scrambling. North Korean worker prosecutions in Apr and May 2026 put hiring fraud on boards' agendas, while 3-second voice cloning and virtual-camera injection attacks defeat casual video interviews.
revenue_model: $60-120 per verified person per year, $1-3K per month platform fee, and $250 per supplier onboarding. Add a paid $2K 'ITAR access audit' as an entry product.
non_obvious_insight: In space the compliance object is not employee identity but nationality-scoped access to technical data. The unbuilt gap is attribute-based access control fed by identity proof into CAD and PLM systems. These startups fear DDTC and DoD audits and investor diligence more than hackers, so they buy compliance evidence rather than security.

Sell a $2K ITAR access audit (export the Drive, GitHub and PLM permission lists and flag foreign-person exposures) to 5 startups via investor and accelerator introductions in Colorado Springs, Los Angeles and Huntsville. Convert audits to per-seat subscriptions before the Nov 2026 CMMC milestone.

Biggest structural risks:

2. Legal and product risk. The Clifford Chance settlement ($132K) shows DOJ IER penalizes employers who over-apply ITAR into citizenship discrimination. ITAR does not require hiring only US persons. Under INA 274B, employers cannot demand specific documents or run citizenship checks unevenly. A biometric 'US person' scanner sold to HR is legally delicate. Verifying green-card, asylee and refugee status by document scan is harder than a citizen passport check, and the I-9 already exists as the system of record.
3. Easy DIY. An IT admin can put an I-9-derived flag into an Okta group, so the paid value must be audit and drift detection plus the exception workflow, not the attribute itself.
